The president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, confirmed on Wednesday that his forces had attacked and destroyed the luxurious mansion of one of the main leaders of Haiti's criminal gangs, known as "Jeff" Larose. A German state data regulator has opened an investigation on Wednesday into Deutsche Bank following a massive data leak. The authority is investigating possible data protection violations.

Following the massive data breach that leaked over 15 million internal records, the office of the commissioner for data protection in Hesse has said on Wednesday that it has launched a probe into Deutsche Bank.

Alexander Rossnagel, the data protection commissioner, said he will check whether the bank had appropriate data protection measures and if the leak was reported in a timely fashion.

"I am investigating whether Deutsche Bank promptly notified the affected individuals," Rossnagel said.

Whistleblowers leaked internal documents to a group of international media, revealing that the bank had reportedly ignored repeated internal warnings about money laundering, corruption or sanctions violations.

Among the bank's clients are Russian oligarchs, US President Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Deutsche Bank CEO admits errors

"When you look at the events today, you naturally question whether something could have been done differently," CEO of Deutsche Bank, Christian Sewing, told German newspaper Handelsblatt.

"Looking back, you can always say that at a certain point in time you might have been able to prioritise differently," Sewing told Handelsblatt.

When asked whether he took internal warnings seriously, Sewing refuted: "During the customer review, I asked whether a private customer needs the same complex process as a large company with 300 subsidiaries," Handelsblatt reports.

"That doesn't mean I wanted to put risks aside."

A blow to Deutsche Bank's reputation

Although Deutsche Bank said the matters "date back many years" and that it had reinforced its controls, the leak has dealt consequential damage to the bank's reputation, sending its share down.

The bank claims it proactively informed the appropriate authorities about the leak and that testing found no account information, login credentials or payment data were accessed.

While the probe won't investigate the documents, it will assess the technical and organisational measures put in place to judge if they were appropriate.

The US Defence Secretary met Delcy Rodríguez in Caracas ahead of a planned visit to Colombia, where he is due to discuss bilateral security cooperation.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela on Wednesday, state TV reported, during an unexpected visit to Caracas.

Hegseth was received by Venezuela's interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, in the capital ahead of a planned visit to Colombia later Wednesday.

"We see this as a renewal of our defence partnership and an opportunity for our two great armed forces to work together," Hegseth said, according to footage broadcast by VTV, Venezuela's state television channel.

The trip, which had not been publicly announced by the Pentagon, marks another step in the rapprochement between Washington and Caracas following the capture in January of Nicolás Maduro.

What does the agreement include?

The cooperation agreement announced by Hegseth and Rodríguez provides for the resumption of technical and military cooperation between Washington and Caracas, which had been suspended for years amid deteriorating diplomatic relations between the two countries.

According to the Venezuelan leader, one of the main objectives is to strengthen the training of Venezuelan armed forces personnel through joint training and cooperation programmes. Rodríguez said the initiative would help improve the military's preparedness to respond to shared threats.

The agreement also aims to improve the operational equipment available to Venezuelan forces and provide access to new technologies. So far, neither government has provided details on the timeline for implementing the agreement, the resources to be allocated or the specific mechanisms through which cooperation will take place.

Washington and Caracas strengthen ties

Rodríguez took power after Maduro was captured, although her continued leadership of the country remains shrouded in uncertainty. Her interim mandate expired in July and there is still no announced date for the next presidential election.

The rapprochement between Washington and Caracas has also been marked by agreements over Venezuelan oil and by the United States' strategy against drug trafficking in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which has caused the deaths of at least 240 people since September 2025 in attacks on vessels suspected of carrying drugs.

Hegseth's visit is part of efforts by Donald Trump's administration to expand its influence in Venezuela. The defence secretary is the third member of Trump's cabinet to travel to the country this year, following trips by the interior and energy secretaries, focused on Venezuela's oil and mineral resources.

GAO a desfășurat testele în perioada decembrie 2025 – octombrie 2026. Ca răspuns la solicitările făcute de investigatori, două dintre platformele au elaborat planuri pentru construirea și detonarea unui dispozitiv exploziv improvizat cu scopul de a provoca numeroase victime. Celelalte două platforme au elaborat planuri pentru utilizarea dronelor sau a armelor de foc în vederea atacării rețelei electrice, conform raportului.

“Fiecare dintre aceste platforme a furnizat informații detaliate care ar putea fi utilizate pentru a desfășura atacuri, precum ținte specifice, locații, momentul și metodele de atac. Fiecare platformă a avut nevoie de mai puțin de 12 ore pentru a genera planuri de atac”, a constatat GAO. 

Într-unul dintre teste, una dintre platforme a sugerat închirierea unui vehicul și achiziționarea de resurse dintr-un magazin situat pe traseul către locația vizată. Acesta a recomandat o dată și o oră concrete pentru atac, deoarece erau programate evenimente publice la care era probabil să se adune mai mulți oameni, se arată în raport.

În cazul testelor privind atacurile asupra stațiilor electrice, una dintre platforme a sugerat utilizarea dronelor, iar alta a propus folosirea armelor de foc împotriva unor stații din apropierea unui aeroport american. Au fost puse la dispoziție inclusiv hărți și imagini.

O platformă a refuzat inițial să ofere informații detaliate despre construirea și detonarea unui dispozitiv exploziv. Totuși, investigatorii au reușit să ocolească mecanismele de protecție și să obțină informațiile solicitate. Celelalte teste au avut rezultate similare.

GAO s-a consultat cu mai mulți experți și a vizitat locațiile propuse de platformele AI pentru a verifica acuratețea planurilor furnizate. În urma verificărilor, au fost identificat și erori, inclusiv drumuri reprezentate incorect și ziduri înalte care ar fi îngreunat observarea unor ținte.

Senatoarea democrată Maggie Hassan, care va prelua conducerea Comisiei pentru Securitate Internă a Senatului în ianuarie, a cerut GAO să investigheze modul în care inteligența artificială disponibilă publicului larg poate fi utilizată în scopuri rău intenționate. Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said the latest EU agreement to accelerate permitting procedures is a step forward for clean power and infrastructure to revamp the bloc's obsolete power grid and boost electrification — even if financing the power grid remains yet another obstacle.

Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen welcomed the recent deal struck by EU lawmakers on permits for energy infrastructure and clean power, describing it as a major win towards integrating more renewable electricity into Europe's energy system and allowing consumers to switch from gas and oil to electricity.

Speaking to Euronews' Europe Tonight, Jørgensen explained that getting those permits can take five years or even a decade, making lengthy approval processes one of the biggest hurdles to electrification.

The deal struck on Wednesday between the EU co-legislators, the European Parliament and the European Council, seeks to bring those permitsdown to just six months for most projects, a significant push intended to unlock investment and help electricity networks keep pace with growing demand.

"This is about making sure that we have the infrastructure to actually electrify our societies, to get the renewable energy into our systems so that we can drive our cars on electricity, we can have heat pumps and so forth," Jørgensen said.

Critics argue that faster permits do not automatically mean cheaper electricity, citing the lack of investment in infrastructure and the fact that network expansion will still have to be paid for.

EU countries are currently discussing the proposal, which has raised some divergences. Sweden pushed back hard, arguing Brussels would redirect money paid by Swedish power consumers and grid operators to fund electricity grids elsewhere in Europe instead of benefiting Stockholm.

Hailing electrification as a new climate doctrine, the Commissioner argued that expanding renewables, improving energy efficiency and connecting national electricity markets would help bring down energy costs.

"The main way of bringing down prices is to deploy more renewables, because renewables are cheaper than the fossil alternative," he said.

Europe has saved more than €30 billion annually through cross-border electricity connections, Jørgensen added, arguing that the potential for further savings remains much greater.

MEP Niels Fuglsang (S&D/Denmark), leading the file in the Parliament, described the deal to speed up the granting of permits as a "very important step".

The Danish lawmaker said the agreement will allow for faster rollout of renewables and grid infrastructure, to the benefit of our citizens, to mitigate climate change and to boost the EU's competitiveness.

A difficult winter exposes Europe's fossil fuel vulnerability

Despite the celebrations in Brussels over the agreement on permits, the Commission's longer-term electrification strategy is unfolding against an immediate energy security challenge. The deal struck on Wednesday won't alleviate energy prices in the short term.

With tensions in the Middle East threatening supplies and markets, the energy Commissioner warned that Europeans should not expect energy prices to return quickly to normal, even if the geopolitical situation stabilises.

"We don't even know if they will come down. What we do know is that it's a very unstable winter that we are going into (...) We also know that even if there's a normalisation of the situation, it'll take months for the prices to normalise," Jørgensen added.

The warning suggests Brussels is preparing for another winter in which households and businesses could face sustained pressure from energy costs, reinforcing the political argument for reducing dependence on imported oil and gas.

The Commissioner urged consumers to switch from gas and oil boilers to heat pumps, replace combustion-engine cars with electric vehicles and improve home insulation.

"We probably have to prepare, or not probably. We unfortunately, for sure, have to prepare for a difficult winter," Jørgensen said.

Vicepremierul Marian Neacșu primește atribuții comparabile cu cele ale unui prim-ministru de facto.

El va aviza proiectele de acte normative cu impact bugetar și va coordona toate ministerele conduse de colegii săi de partid.

Portofoliile exceptate sunt finanțele, externele, energia, educația și cultura.

Decizia semnată de premierul Luca Niculescu a fost publicată astăzi în Monitorul Oficial.

Ea stabilește noile atribuții ale lui Marian Neacșu, cel dintâi ministru de Interne de după 1989 cu o condamnare definitivă la activ: el a primit o pedeapsă cu suspendare pentru conflict de interese, dar a fost între timp reabilitat.

Dan Cărbunaru, purtătorul de cuvânt al Guvernului, a fost întrebat de ce era necesară de această decizie.

A răspuns că actualul cabinet are un singur vicepremier, spre deosebire de cei cinci de dinainte.

În termeni birocratici, explicația are trei cuvinte: cumul de atribuții.

Marian Neacșu mai coordonează cancelaria premierului și Secretariatul General al Guvernului, sub autoritatea căruia funcționează – între altele – companiile de stat Transelectrica și Tranzgaz.

Eurodeputatul Siegfried Mureşan e de părere că Luca Niculescu devine astfel premierul cu cea mai redusă influenţă asupra propriului Guvern de la Revoluţie încoace, iIar deputata USR Oana Ţoiu a spus că PSD preia, de fapt, și rolul de prim-ministru.

Încă o comisie de anchetă

Liberalii și useriștii încep să simtă gustul opoziției – nu numai convocări intempestive la DNA sau plângeri penale pe tema contractelor din programul SAFE, ci și anchete parlamentare.

Deputații și senatorii se pregătesc să înființeze o comisie care să verifice de ce mașini ale Serviciului de Protecție și Pază au fost folosite la finalul săptămânii trecute la nunta din Oradea a fiicei lui Ilie Bolojan.

O parte a invitaților  – printre care s-au numărat politicieni și oameni de afaceri – ar fi ajuns de la aeroport la localul unde a avut loc petrecerea cu mașini de la SPP.

Prezent aseară în platoul Digi24, Ilie Bolojan nu a spus clar dacă mașinile serviciului au fost sau nu folosite în acest scop.

S-a limitat la a se declara victima unor hărțuiri și a unui „festival de minciuni”.

Cererea de înființare a comisiei de anchetă a fost depusă de parlamentari de la PSD, AUR, SOS și din grupul neafiliaților.

Forul parlamentar nu poate să aplice eventuale sancțiuni, ci doar să propună măsuri.

În august, Parlamentul a înființat – de exemplu – o comisie care a anchetat detaliile unei întâlniri dintre Ilie Bolojan președinta Curții Constituționale, Simina Tănăsescu.

La scurt timp după acea discuție, CCR era așteptată să se pronunțe asupra unei dispute între Guvern și instanța supremă, condusă de Lia Savonea.

Comisia și-a încheiat activitatea fără vreo concluzie clară, dar cu propunerea ca Simina Tănăsescu să fie sancționată.

Nunta fiicei președintelui PNL a stârnit interes în contextul în care, cu aproximativ două săptămâni în urmă, numeroși lideri ai PSD își etalaseră luxul la un botez – al copilului lui Alfred Simonis, președinte al Consiliului Județean Timiș.

Premierul, înlocuit la Berlin

Președintele Nicușor Dan ia parte mâine, în Berlin, la o nouă reuniune a Coaliției Voluntarilor: grupul de state europene condus de Franța și de Marea Britanie care promovează un acord de pace în Ucraina favorabil țării vecine.

Surse guvernamentale citate de HotNews spun că, inițial, România ar fi urmat să fie reprezentată de premierul Luca Niculescu.

Deplasarea lui, însă, a fost anulată.

Nicușor Dan face eforturi susținute de a se apropia de administrația Trump – la reuniunea de mâine din Berlin vor lua parte emisarii președintelui american în Ucraina și Rusia, Jared Kushner și Steve Witkoff.

Într-un comunicat al Cotroceniului se spune că un viitor acord de pace trebuie să țină cont de interesele de securitate ale Europei: „O pace durabilă în Ucraina presupune restaurarea deplină a securității la Marea Neagră”.

Numeroase atacuri cu dronă asupra vaselor comerciale din Marea Neagră au făcut din aceasta cea mai riscantă rută de transport pe apă din lume: anul acesta, au murit aproape patruzeci de marinari.

Compania daneză Maersk, specializată în transportul maritim, tocmai ce-a introdus două taxe noi pentru Bulgaria, Georgia și România – zona maritimă a Mării Negre a fost desemnată drept una cu risc de război, ceea ce presupune cheltuieli mai mari de operare pentru navele care activează în regiune.

„The big Three”, întâlnire în China

Ucraina, pe de altă parte, e una dintre temele majore ale întâlnirii de mâine dintre președinții Chinei, Statelor Unite și Rusiei.

Donald Trump a ajuns astăzi în Shenzen, unde a dat deja mâna cu Xi Jinping și Vladimir Putin.

Cei trei iau parte la Forumul Cooperării Economice Asia-Pacific – APEC. Întâlnirea oficială e programată mîine, la 08:30, ora României.

Ea a fost deja comparată cu Conferința de la Ialta din 1945, când Roosevelt, Churchill și Stalin au negociat ordinea internațională de după cel de-al doilea război mondial.

Totuși, în ciuda simbolisticii, Vladimir Putin e profund dependent de China în momentul de față, iar republicanii lui Donald Trump au suferit o înfrângere usturătoare la alegerile de la mijlocul mandatului prezidențial: din ianuarie, ambele camere ale Congresului Statelor Unite vor fi dominate de opoziția democrată.

Înaintea summitului de mâine, comerțul global liber și deschis a fost apărat cel puternic de către liderul comunist: Xi Jinnping a criticat protecționismul economic și a anunțat că Beijingul are de gând, spre deosebire de Statele Unite, să reducă tarifele vamale.

Putin, la rândul său, susține că sancțiunile occidentale impuse Rusiei după invadarea Ucrainei și-ar fi pierdut eficiența.

Cel care i-a dat replica a fost premierul Canadei: Mark Carney l-a îndemnat pe președintele Rusiei să-și întrebe instituțiile financiare și prietenii oligarhi dacă sancțiunile sunt sau nu o chestiune de domeniul trecutului.

The New York Democrat secured 251 votes in favour and 11 against, but faces pressure from progressive lawmakers demanding commitments on healthcare, immigration and other key issues.

Hakeem Jeffries is one step closer to making history as the first Black Speaker of the US House of Representatives, after Democrats nominated him for the powerful role despite a small but vocal group of progressive dissenters.

Jeffries, who has served as House minority leader and leader of the House Democratic Caucus since 2023, secured the nod following a closed-door vote. 251 voted for his nomination, compared with 11 against. The move came ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January.

Many of those who voted “no” are a group of progressive newcomers, who said in a statement that there is “still work to be done” to ensure their priorities.

Jeffries, who hails from New York, ran unopposed but says he is taking nothing for granted. He faces a restive party eager for a change after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and his underlings.

Democrats, both established and newly-elected, say they’ve been flooded with phone calls and social media posts demanding a fresh start.

Last week, protesters heckled Jeffries during a Democratic conference in Denver, Colorado.

Those opposing Jeffries, including some backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, said conversations are ongoing about his potential new role.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they said in a joint statement.

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

He was nominated alongside Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would also be historic firsts, Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. Both also ran unopposed.

The trio will face another vote when the new Congress convenes for the first time on 3 January, 2027.

Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar have risen together, as a team, as the first new generation of leaders of the post-Pelosi era and will likely serve as leaders in the majority for the first time.

When Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California decided to step aside from leadership in 2022 after the party's electoral defeat that handed Republicans the majority, it set the stage for this very era.

Meanwhile, a similar upheaval with Democrats angling for change is happening in the Senate, where Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, a Democrat who’s been the senior United States senator for the state since 2017.

Another batch of EU sanctions targeting Russian banks, oil refineries and Russia's "shadow fleet" is expected later this month. But are sanctions actually effective against Moscow?

The EU's foreign ministers have approved another sanctions package targeting Russian banks, oil refineries, and its "shadow fleet".

This latest batch of sanctions targets almost 150 additional individuals and entities, while the EU's 22nd economic sanctions package is expected later this month.

The EU has slapped sanctions on around 4,600 individuals and entities and frozen more than €28 billion in private assets since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

What sanctions are actually effective against Moscow?

Sanctions appear to be more effective against Russia than others.

Analysts say that oil import bans and export controls on Western tech hit the country hardest, because they deliver a blow to its economy and its ability to make sophisticated military equipment.

However, Russia can exploit trade loopholes and use its so-called illicit "shadow fleet" to export oil.

"If you are somebody who is inside Russia and who wants to get the sanctioned goods, it's not that difficult. A lot of this comes through third countries like Kazakhstan, Turkey, Armenia, Hong Kong and so on. And you don't even have to hide them, because on the Russian side of the border it's legal," Konstantin Egorov, associate professor of economics at the University of Antwerp, told Euronews Verify.

Who is really behind Europe's airline bomb scares?

Today's episode also focuses on the latest bomb threats.

In just five days, more than 50 flights across Europe were caught up in a wave of bomb threats.

Aircraft were diverted, fighter jets were scrambled, and passengers faced lengthy delays, but searches of the plane found no explosives.

"Unfortunately, there's very little hard evidence that it's sort of directly linked to Russia. We've got speculation in popular reporting, including some, you know, alleged reports from anonymous security officials close to the investigation," said Rhys Jones, analysis output manager at Osprey Flight Solutions.

"But what I think we can say is that it's consistent with the operational intentions and the sort of tactics we've seen from Russia previously."

What could these bomb threats achieve?

This kind of disruption affects different fronts.

The aim is to impose economic costs and undermine the political order of the countries affected.

"I think it does fit into a wider pattern. We can see that all kinds of infrastructure are being targeted," said Guntram Wolff, senior fellow at Bruegel.

"But more importantly, it's really about the political cost that comes with it. It is part of an information campaign, part of a political campaign against the political system, against the existing political order. And it really aims at destabilising our countries."

An activist criticised a French public broadcaster after a presenter revealed her marriage to a senior TV executive, sparking controversy over transparency rules and political reactions.

French public broadcaster franceinfo has faced criticism after a presenter revealed feminist activist Anne-Cécile Mailfert's marriage to a senior television executive during a live broadcast on Monday.

Before she could speak, the presenter introduced her as the wife of the number two at public television giant France Télévisions.

Visibly outraged, Mailfert responded, "So what?", calling the disclosure "absolutely scandalous". She then challenged a male journalist on the panel, asking, "Who is your partner?"

Transparency rules spark controversy

The incident followed the introduction of new transparency guidelines aimed at preventing conflicts of interest within France's public broadcasters.

While franceinfo initially defended the disclosure as consistent with the rules, it later acknowledged that Mailfert should have been informed beforehand.

Mailfert, who was heard shouting as she left the studio, addressed the incident on Instagram on Tuesday, saying it had deeply affected her.

"Yesterday, I experienced something that hurt me deeply," she wrote.

The activist insisted that she is "deeply committed" to the principles of "professional ethics, transparency, and integrity".

"However, these principles must address a genuine risk of a conflict of interest - one that is clearly defined - and the individuals involved must be informed."

Yannick Letranchant, franceinfo's head of ethics and transparency, acknowledged the challenge of balancing "necessary transparency" and the risk of "relegating an individual" to the status of being the partner of someone else.

Political reactions ahead of French presidential election

The controversy has prompted reactions from across France's political spectrum, including hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon but also parliament speaker Yael Braun-Pivet.

"A woman holds her own convictions, fights her own battles, and speaks for herself. This should be a given in 2026," Braun-Pivet said.

The dispute comes ahead of France's presidential election next year, as France Télévisions faces continued scrutiny over its political impartiality.

The public broadcaster has repeatedly been accused of left-wing bias by the far right, while also facing criticism from Mélenchon's hard-left movement.

French real estate company Nexity presented the first apartment building of its kind on Tuesday, which is designed to maintain an interior temperature between 20 °C and 26 °C without heating or air conditioning.

Almost brutalist in style, this new white and cubic building is the first of its kind in France. Its cutting-edge design allows it to regulate its interior temperature without using heaters or air conditioning.

In Lyon, French real estate company Nexity and Austrian architectural firm Baumschlager Eberle presented on Tuesday their new seven-story-high project of 23 housing units in the ever-transforming Confluence neighbourhood.

No need for air conditioning in the summer or heating in the winter; that's the realtor's promise. The building is designed to maintain an interior temperature of 20 to 22°C in the winter and 26 to 28°C during heatwaves.

An Austrian concept

Seeking a response to the energy and climate crisis, Austrian architect Dietmar Eberle designed a building capable of letting sunlight in to retain the heat, called "22-26" in reference to the interior temperature it should maintain.

This cutting-edge technology that has yet to prove its effectiveness, is based on the building material's inertia.

"These play a major role and have been selected for a common characteristic: their ability to store and release energy," Anne Speicher, director of the Baumschlager Eberle agency, told online French media Vert.

"An insulating envelope, constructed from Monomur bricks (a hollow-core terracotta structure), concrete and a lime render, helps to retain heat or coolness inside homes," reports the French media.

The heat is "retained" by the walls and floors that are twice as thick as France's average, 61 centimetres compared to around 30 in average.

Two layers of hollow bricks interspersed with glass wool insulation give the building a quite massive appearance while also protecting it from direct sunlight thanks to large recesses.

The concept also relies on innovative construction planning and on an automatic slat system controlled by multiple sensors.

Wooden slats installed in each housing unit automatically open and close to air out the apartment regarding its "temperature, humidity, air quality and weather," explains Nexity in a press release.

"Residents can also monitor them themselves. Auxiliary heaters, which are required by regulation, only turn on during extreme weather events or following a prolonged period when the property has been unoccupied."

Residents act as heaters

The greatly insulated apartments retain the heat produced by the residents' bodies, "we are the heaters of the home — us and what we do," Cédric Hatat, Programme Manager at Nexity Auvergne Bourgogne told French broadcaster BFM Business.

The heat produced by cooking, showering or electric appliances will also be trapped in the apartments, reducing energy bills by 80%, according to Nexity's CEO Véronique Bédague. This would save every resident €380 a year for a three-room apartment.

Each apartment is still equipped with heaters and a double-flow mechanical ventilation system, as required by French law. The realtor claims this has raised the construction cost by 15% to connect the building to the city's heating system.

This technology is also supposed to cut energy consumption associated with thermal comfort by 73%, reducing carbon emissions by 65% over 50 years.

High construction cost

The Austrian agency has already built two of these "22-26" type buildings in Switzerland and Germany, but it's the first one in France.

Its reproducibility is uncertain because of high construction costs, "this project cannot be replicated on a large scale," elected ecologist metropolitan councillor at the Métropole de Lyon, Renaud Payre, told Vert.

"The cost of materials, the highly sophisticated home automation system on which it is based… The 22-26 is quite simply too complex to establish itself as a standard model for construction."

"It is designed to serve as a showcase for sustainable housing and to encourage the development of local supply chains," Payre told Vert.

The ecologist councillor claims that housing renovation remains the best way to improve apartments' energy consumption.

"Of course, you can pick up a few techniques or ideas here and there, but as things stand, you cannot turn a draughty building into an energy-efficient one using state-of-the-art, very expensive home automation systems," Payre told Vert.

Other cities have been won over by the concept; the building's realtor, Nexity, plans to complete the construction of a similar 22-26 project in La Garenne-Colombes, near Paris, in 2028. This other test project building that will host 80 housing units is set to gauge the effectiveness of this concept.

Cei doi lideri au dat mâna și s-au îmbrățișat în fața camerelor de filmat. Primirea călduroasă organizată de Xi Jinping pentru Trump este considerată un gest diplomatic prin care liderul chinez încearcă să creeze o atmosferă favorabilă discuțiilor. 

În mod obișnuit, liderii străini sunt întâmpinați la sosire de miniștri sau alți oficiali de rang înalt, nu personal de șeful statului gazdă. Potrivit presei chineze, este primul astfel de gest al unui lider suprem al Chinei în aproape 70 de ani, precedentul cunoscut datând din 1959, când Mao Zedong l-a primit la aeroport pe liderul sovietic Nikita Hrușciov. Xi a explicat că a dorit să răspundă astfel gestului făcut de Trump în septembrie, când președintele american l-a întâmpinat personal la aeroport în timpul vizitei sale în SUA.

Ulterior, Trump s-a întâlnit și cu Vladimir Putin, cei doi salutându-se și schimbând câteva amabilități înaintea unei recepții oficiale. Momentul marchează prima întâlnire față în față dintre președintele american și cel rus din august 2025, când Putin a vizitat Alaska pentru discuții privind războiul din Ucraina. Întâlnirea de atunci nu a dus la un acord de pace.

Potrivit purtătorului de cuvânt al Kremlinului, Dmitri Peskov, Trump și Putin nu au avut miercuri o discuție propriu-zisă, ci doar s-au salutat. Cei doi urmează însă să aibă joi o întrevedere bilaterală, separată de discuțiile cu Xi Jinping, potrivit unui oficial american citat de Associated Press. Aceasta ar fi prima lor întâlnire individuală de la summitul din Alaska.

Discuțiile trilaterale de joi sunt programate să dureze cel mult o oră, a precizat Peskov, citat de agențiile de presă ruse. Nu a fost publicată o agendă oficială, însă Trump a declarat anterior că războiul din Ucraina va fi unul dintre subiectele abordate.

Posibilitatea ca soarta războiului din Ucraina să fie discutată fără participarea reprezentanților de la Kiev a stârnit îngrijorări în rândul autorităților ucrainene. Președintele Volodimir Zelenski a avertizat în repetate rânduri că nu trebuie luate decizii privind Ucraina fără participarea acesteia. Ministrul ucrainean de Externe, Andrii Sîbiga, a cerut miercuri Statelor Unite și Chinei să folosească influența pe care o au asupra Moscovei pentru a determina Rusia să pună capăt războiului, aflat aproape de împlinirea a cinci ani.

În paralel, emisarii americani Steve Witkoff și Jared Kushner sunt așteptați joi la Berlin, unde vor participa la discuții privind Ucraina alături de reprezentanții așa-numitei „Coaliții a Voinței”, grupul de state care susțin Kievul. Întâlnirea este organizată de Germania, Franța și Marea Britanie și va include discuții cu cancelarul german Friedrich Merz, președintele francez Emmanuel Macron și premierul britanic Andy Burnham. Potrivit unui oficial german, momentul reuniunii a fost ales astfel încât aliații europeni ai Ucrainei să poată reacționa rapid la eventualele rezultate ale discuțiilor din China.

Beijingul nu a confirmat dacă războiul din Ucraina va fi un subiect central al summitului. China susține oficial că este neutră în conflict, însă Ucraina și aliații săi occidentali acuză Beijingul că sprijină indirect efortul militar rus, inclusiv prin exporturi de tehnologii și componente cu dublă utilizare, care pot avea atât aplicații civile, cât și militare. Autoritățile chineze au respins aceste acuzații.

Putin a ajuns la Shenzhen cu câteva ore înaintea lui Trump și a avut aproximativ două ore de discuții cu Xi Jinping. Cei doi au reafirmat apropierea dintre țările lor și dorința de a consolida cooperarea economică și militară. Xi a descris relația bilaterală drept „stabilă ca un munte, de neclintit în fața furtunilor”.

Summitul de la Shenzhen are loc într-un context internațional tensionat, în care cele trei puteri încearcă să își negocieze interesele într-o serie de dosare majore. Analiștii evidențiază că, deși durata redusă a discuțiilor trilaterale și lipsa unei agende publice lasă multe întrebări deschise, întâlnirea este importantă prin simplul fapt că îi aduce pentru prima dată la aceeași masă pe liderii Statelor Unite, Chinei și Rusiei.

The party leadership will submit the proposal to the political assembly, where it is expected to secure approval. SNS could make a comeback, provided it meets certain conditions.

The European People’s Party (EPP) is expected to suspend the membership of Serbia’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) at its next political assembly, scheduled for December.

The EPP presidency, headed by Germany’s Manfred Weber, is set to propose the suspension following an internal scrutiny process launched more than a year ago, EPP sources told Euronews.

The centre-right political family has long been on a collision course with the party of former Serbian president Aleksandar Vučić over its ties to Russia and its violent crackdown on protests.

Frustration within the EPP has grown in recent months, culminating in renewed calls for action following the granting of state honoursand the presence of senior Serbian officials at the funeral of Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić.

A convicted war criminal known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, Mladić died in a UN detention facility in The Hague in late August, aged 84.

The political assembly, comprising delegates from EPP-affiliated parties, must endorse the presidency’s proposal at its meeting in Brussels on 7–8 December. The number of delegates allocated to each party is determined by its performance in the most recent European elections, ensuring that national parties are represented in proportion to their electoral strength.

“An overwhelming majority of the EPP is in favour of the suspension,” a member of the presidency told Euronews, considering the outcome all but certain.

The presidency has been considering the move for several months but wanted to wait for the outcome of the Serbian elections before putting it forward.

SNS, which had dominated Serbia’s political landscape until this year, lost October’s parliamentary election to the Student List and is set to enter opposition for the first time in nearly 14 years.

If suspended, the party would have one year to meet certain conditions established by the assembly to be reinstated, an EPP official told Euronews.

SNS has been an EPP associate member since 2016. The party was contacted for comment but had not responded by the time of publication.

Waymo has taken its driverless taxis off highways across the United States after California temporarily banned the ride-hailing service from its freeways over safety concerns.

The company, a subsidiary of Google’s parent company Alphabet, has "temporarily restricted freeway operations", a spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday.

As well as California, the pause covers highway rides in the other cities where Waymo offers them, including Phoenix in Arizona, Austin in Texas and Miami in Florida.

The spokesperson said the suspension would allow the company to "evaluate our performance" after the incidents in California, adding that Waymo prioritises safety.

The move is likely to add to the debate over the risks of driverless taxis, which are beginning to expand into Europe.

Waymo has been testing its vehicles in London, United Kingdom, since last year and plans to expand to Munich in Germany and Madrid in Spain in 2027.

One of the incidents went viral last week. A video filmed on Interstate 280 in San Francisco showed a Waymo vehicle approaching at speed and trying to overtake two California Highway Patrol cars. The police cars had their lights flashing to deliberately slow traffic behind a slow-moving construction truck.

The episode led California’s Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), which is responsible for road safety, to temporarily ban Waymo vehicles from the state’s highways from 11 November.

According to the DMV, a separate incident also led to the decision. In that case, "three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure" in the San Francisco Bay Area, an agency spokesperson said.

"Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," the statement said.

The restrictions "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates ... it has taken effective corrective actions", it added.

Waymo stressed that no one was injured and no collisions occurred in the construction zone incident.

The two storms combined meant that several records for maximum wind gusts and rainfall were broken in the first 12 days of November, according to the Portuguese Institute for the Sea and the Atmosphere (IPMA).

Although storm Charles did not have the catastrophic consequences the Portuguese government had previously anticipated, this depression, together with the earlier system Bruna, led to record levels of rain and wind for the month of November, according to the Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA).

IPMA has now published its report on the two depressions (source in Portuguese) that affected mainland Portugal and Madeira between 7 and 12 November and recorded several records. Both daily rainfall and maximum wind gusts reached new record highs for this month. Each of these records was broken four times during the period.

As for accumulated rainfall over the first 12 days of the month, it was well above the "climatological norm", that is, the average recorded between 1991 and 2020, at several weather stations, especially in the centre and south of mainland Portugal.

The stations at Mora and Mértola, both in the Alentejo region, stand out, where rainfall was more than 180% above normal, as does Tapada da Ajuda in Lisbon, with a 174% increase. At several of these stations, the rain recorded during the first 12 days of November accounted for more than 25% of the total measured so far in 2026.

Regarding the warnings issued for the 10th, when the entire mainland territory was placed on alert and people were advised not to leave home, IPMA considers that "the storm produced gusts that were lower than initially forecast, though still consistent with a yellow warning, in the order of 70 to 90 km/h along the southern coast. At some of the most exposed locations, according to IPMA stations at Cabo da Roca, Fóia and Loulé (Cavalos do Caldeirão), values compatible with an orange warning were reached, with the strongest gust of the event hitting 123 km/h at the Fóia station". As for rainfall, IPMA says that the figures "justified a red warning for six-hour accumulation (> 60 mm) at several stations in the Lisbon district".

EU auditors warn that slow regulation, patchy enforcement and outdated food and drinking water safety limits are leaving Europeans exposed to harmful chemicals, six years after Brussels pledged to phase out their non-essential uses.

The European Union has failed to deliver on its pledge to phase out harmful "forever chemicals", known as PFAS, because of sluggish regulation, weak enforcement and outdated safety limits, according to a damning report by the European Court of Auditors (ECA).

Six years after the European Commission vowed to eliminate non-essential uses of PFAS, thousands of substances remain largely unregulated, while national authorities are failing to check whether existing restrictions are being respected, the auditors said.

PFAS are widely used in consumer and industrial products, from non-stick cookware and waterproof textiles to medical equipment and food packaging. They break down extremely slowly and have been linked to cancer, reproductive problems and weakened immune responses.

An awareness campaign involving EU ministers and Commissioners last year found that everyone who underwent blood tests tested positive for PFAS. Yet Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has repeatedly declined to meet EU citizens affected by PFAS pollution in recent years.

“These chemicals may last forever, but there are ways to limit their harmful effects on people and the environment,” said Joëlle Elvinger, the ECA member who led the audit.

“The EU must tackle this problem firmly and without delay to defuse this ticking time bomb before it is too late.”

The auditors found that while the EU had made political commitments and funded research, it had failed to translate these efforts into effective protection for citizens.

The audit comes a day after a separate investigation by campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO) accused the chemical industry of stepping up its lobbying efforts to water down the EU's proposed PFAS restrictions, potentially leaving large parts of the sector exempt from the planned ban.

"The ‘forever pollution’ crisis caused by the manufacture, use, and disposal of PFAS is getting worse. It is clear that citizens across Europe (and beyond) are contaminated with these chemicals, some at far higher levels than is considered safe," reads the CEO's report.

Sluggish regulation and weak enforcement

Although the EU was among the first to restrict PFAS, its regulatory framework has struggled to keep pace with the scale of the problem.

The ECA audit said the regulatory process is "too slow" to address chemicals that can persist in the environment for generations. Assessing the hazards of individual PFAS takes an average of six years, the ECA auditors said, while adopting restrictions takes almost five years.

The substance-by-substance approach has also encouraged so-called "regrettable substitution", whereby banned chemicals are replaced with others with similar properties and potentially similar risks.

A proposal to restrict PFAS as a group, covering thousands of substances and uses, was submitted in 2023 by five European countries. But its complexity means the scientific assessment alone is expected to take around four years, before the Commission can move towards a final decision.

Even where restrictions are in place, enforcement is patchy. A third of EU member states carried out no targeted checks on PFAS compliance between 2020 and 2025, the auditors found.

Limited laboratory capacity, high testing costs and competing priorities were among the reasons cited by national authorities for the lack of enforcement.

EU chemicals agency split

Neither the Commission nor the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) has a comprehensive overview of national enforcement efforts, leaving implementation fragmented and heavily reliant on companies policing themselves.

ECHA has already backed a ban on PFAS, although the final decision rests with the Commission.

However, inside the Helsinki-based agency, two scientific committees — risk assessment and socio-economic analysis — held somewhat divergent views, with the latter seeking to ensure that industries reliant on some PFAS wouldn't be affected.

ECHA's socio-economic committee is expected to deliver a final assessment of the impact of a PFAS withdrawal soon. After ECHA's submission, Brussels is under pressure to propose a restriction.

Meanwhile, no new EU restriction procedures have been launched since the universal proposal, apart from measures covering firefighting foams and PFHxA.

Martin Dermine, executive director at the NGO Pesticide Action Network Europe, said PFAS pesticides, beyond their intrinsic toxicity to humans, contaminate groundwater with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), a forever PFAS metabolite.

"TFA levels in drinking water are very high in intensive agriculture areas, and TFA was recently classified as Toxic to Reproduction. It is urgent that the Commission bans all PFAS pesticides," Dermine told Euronews.

PFAS in food and drinking water

The EU's food and drinking water rules are also lagging behind scientific evidence.

Food limits cover only four PFAS in certain products, despite more than 50 different PFAS having been detected in food.

The ECA auditors calculated that if certain foods contained the maximum permitted PFAS level, a person could exceed their tolerable weekly intake after eating only around 7 grams of anchovies, 39 grams of wild salmon, 181 grams of eggs or 237 grams of beef.

According to the ECA audit, five EU countries submitted no food-monitoring data between 2020 and 2024, while the Commission has yet to use the growing database to decide whether existing limits should be revised or extended to other substances and food categories.

"We are not naming and shaming. It’s our job to analyse the data and the legislation and to make our recommendation to the Commission," Elvinger told reporters on Wednesday, as all 27 EU countries were asked to reply to ECA's survey for the audit.

Denmark, Germany, France and the Netherlands account for more than half of all PFAS food-monitoring data submitted to the EU between 2020 and 2024.

Nonetheless, Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania and Slovakia were urged to introduce PFAS checks in their 2026 national food-control plans.

The ECA auditors also found that the Commission had exceeded the five-year review timetable for drinking-water limits, waiting for new World Health Organization recommendations expected in 2027.

Eight of the 25 EU countries responding to the audit had already introduced additional national limits, exposing differences in the level of protection across the bloc.

The ECA is calling on the Commission to accelerate the universal restriction process, overhaul regulatory procedures, strengthen national enforcement and update food and drinking-water limits where justified by scientific evidence.

Most recommendations have deadlines stretching to 2028 or 2029, although the Commission is urged to reach a decision on the universal restriction proposal by 2027.

"Better and faster action is necessary to protect our citizens. We hope the Commission will implement our recommendations," Elvinger told reporters on Wednesday.

Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne will receive the European Lifetime Achievement Award from the European Film Academy, in recognition of their body of work. Euronews Culture sat down with the filmmaking duo to discuss the prize, the perils of AI, and the evolution of European cinema.

Celebrated Belgian filmmakers Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardennes will be the recipients of next year's European Film Awards' Lifetime Achievement Prize. 

The directing duo, famous for their humanist and compassionate dramas, have been two of the leading figures in European independent cinema for almost 40 years. They have won six prizes in Cannes over their illustrious career – including two Palme d'Or awards for Rosetta and L'Enfant (The Child).

Their most recent prize was last year for Jeunes Mères (Young Mothers), which won Best Screenplay on the Croisette. 

Their recognition at the European Film Awards includes winning best documentary in 1997 for Gigi, Monica… Et Bianca and the European screenwriter award in 2011 for Le gamin au vélo (The Kid With A Bike).

Euronews Culture sat down with the Dardenne Brothers to discuss their upcoming EFA prize, the perils of AI in cinema, and the current evolution of European cinema.

Cinema, as well as other art forms can humanise us, even though culture has never put a stop to barbarism. 

Euronews Culture: You will receive the European Film Academy's Lifetime Achievement Award next January. What does this award mean to you?

Luc Dardenne: For us, it’s a great honour to receive this award. I think it reflects the fact that we’ve made films that have had a certain continuity. By that I mean a continuity in our artistic exploration. It’s a bit pretentious to say that about oneself, but anyway, there’s a body of work that’s trying to take shape, and I think that after a certain time, you can indeed say: ‘Well, there’s something rather unique about these two brothers who’ve been making films for about forty years’. Plus, we’re European, so the Academy probably thought: ‘Right, we should honour them!’ (Laughs)

I had the pleasure of speaking with Academy president Juliette Binoche, who told me that one of her aims was to rehumanise society through cinema. What do you make of that statement?

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: One must always be careful with statements, even if they are important. There are many examples throughout history that show us that cinema hasn’t humanised anything at all… But, it can contribute to us being human. It can help us become more human. Certain films can do that. Charlie Chaplin’s films, for example, can help us become more human, that’s for sure. It’s true that in cinema, as well as other art forms can humanise us, even though culture has never put a stop to barbarism.

Her comment reminded me of a definition of cinema that I’ve always liked: that cinema is a machine for generating empathy. It’s a definition that fits your films well, and I was wondering if you can remember the first film that made an impression on you in that respect – one that generated empathy within you?

Luc Dardenne: Among the films that have made an impression on me, as you say, and which have sparked a desire for brotherhood, friendship and mutual support, I’d mention Kenji Mizoguchi’s Sancho The Bailiff. When I first saw it, quite a long time ago now, I did indeed feel a profound human sense of compassion, friendship and closeness to the victims, the oppressed, and the people trying to build a better life for themselves.

There are films like that - films by Bresson, for example. And then sometimes there are some love stories. If I think of Truffaut’s The Woman Next Door, it’s a tragedy, but it also captures human complexity… One can feel a deep friendship, a profound sense of closeness to human beings in a film such as The Woman Next Door. We feel close to these two lovers, close to their story, their inability to love one another and yet love each other. Beyond this impossibility, we experience something very profound and very human.

That is what cinema is all about. It is not a militant language, I would say; it is a complex language. These are complex emotions. Because when Mizoguchi made his film, it was political, as it's a film in which someone breaks free from slavery... But it's also a complex story about human relationships.

You mentioned Charlie Chaplin – any specific examples that spring to mind?

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: All of Chaplin’s films. Because there is such generosity in his films, a constant spirit of civil disobedience in the character of the Tramp, and an enormous faith in life. That’s important too. It’s that sort of cinema that matters. The kind that believes in life – and that’s full of life. Chaplin’s films are full of life - they’re not like funeral dirges, and that’s beautiful. He’s not the only one, of course, but I mentioned Chaplin because he’s a bit of a benchmark for everyone. Everyone knows him, and everyone has seen at least one Chaplin film in their lifetime. Even if you don’t go to the cinema any more, you’ve seen at least one Chaplin film. It’s good that cinema lives on under the watchful eye of the Tramp.

Luc Dardenne: Then there’s Paulette Goddard in the films too, alongside Chaplin (in Modern Times and The Great Dictator). She’s brilliant as well. She brings such life in Modern Times. It’s magnificent.

We don't want actors and actresses to be replaced, or films to be edited by AI. We need to ensure that there remains a sense of humanity in cinema. We’ve got to fight for this.

Over the course of your careers, you’ve presented your films at several festivals, including, of course, Cannes. You’ve been ideally placed to bear witness to the evolution of European cinema. Do you think it’s heading in the right direction?

Luc Dardenne: We are, I would say, living through a time of great upheaval. The current situation is complex for European cinema, world cinema, but also for African cinema – because we always tend to forget about it. For them, however, the situation is more financial and practical in nature. But what is going to happen? I don’t know. As for what the situation actually is, I’m not entirely sure either.

There are several ways of looking at it. I think the perspectives of writers and filmmakers, men and women, will endure. The question is: Will they still have the technical, practical and financial means to express themselves, to criticise, to love, and to make the world love? Will that still be possible? Given the dwindling number of cinemas and the rise of streaming platforms which, whatever people may say, do require a fair amount of standardisation, I’d say that faced with such a complex situation, the only thing I feel certain about is that we’re going to have to fight.

We – the writers, filmmakers and film technicians, the cinema operators and the heads of television channels and streaming platforms as well – are people who love cinema and who do not want artificial intelligence to make films for us. We don't want actors and actresses to be replaced, or films to be edited by AI. We need to ensure that there remains a sense of humanity in cinema. We’ve got to fight for this. We’ve got to refuse to hand over all our data to artificial intelligence.

At the same time, we’ve got to use it as a tool as well, because it’s useful for certain things, but that’s the big issue today. I don’t think cinema is going to disappear as a medium. It’ll still exist – but it needs to reflect a truly human perspective from a woman or a man making a film with living beings. Making a film that’s alive.

Will that still be possible considering the maddening push towards more AI in every aspect of our lives?

Luc Dardenne: I hope so. But we have to fight for it. And freedom, too, because there is freedom in cinema. Filmmakers like Rossellini, Godard and Agnès Varda had great freedom. Will we still be able to find that freedom if the tools dictate the writing and structure of films? So I think we need to be wary of all these new tools. We can use them, but wisely and without believing we’re above them. Otherwise we'll end up being swallowed up by them. And maybe I interpret the award we’re about to receive in this light. We’re craftspeople. We work day after day on films. We do something, redo it, start again... I hope it’s that work, too, that’s being honoured.

If we ever confuse the simulacrum with reality, we’re done for – and society is done for too. 

It does feel as though there’s a new threat to cinema with each passing year – be it Covid, which closed down so many cinemas, or the rise of streaming platforms. Now, it's AI, a technology that could be described as posing an existential threat to cinema as an artform, as well as human creation in general.

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: I don’t know anything about AI, so we must be very careful not to turn conversations into pub debates, so to speak. The other day I heard a doctor from a Belgian hospital talking about how treatment for a certain type of cancer will become increasingly personalised. He explained how artificial intelligence enables them to process a whole range of data and analyse it. He said that without artificial intelligence, you couldn't do that. So, this technology could be something marvellous. But it’s the same with everything – it depends on how we’re going to use it. Of course, there are people whose sole obsession is profit at any cost. It’s propaganda at any cost. They were certainly like that before, so this artificial intelligence will be a means of amplifying their actions and their thirst for profit. But there are others too, for whom it can be a source of help, a working tool. I think that’s what it can be - a working tool.

Luc Dardenne: In medicine, in ecology, in all the areas we need to monitor in relation to climate issues… Artificial intelligence will play a real role, that much is certain. But when it comes to art, to cinema – which is most affected – for us, it’s a mechanical art form. If we ever confuse the simulacrum with reality, we’re done for – and society is done for too.

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: Yes, but the fact that we’re talking about it proves that this isn’t yet the case.

Luc Dardenne: But there are some who would do nothing to stop it because it’s very lucrative, and we have to stand up to them.

If Europe were ever to decide to abolish the ‘cultural exception’ and treat culture as just another commercial product, it would be a real disaster.

Thanks to your films, as well as those by directors such as Emmanuel Marre, Lukas Dhont and Michael Roskam, to name but a few, Belgium has been gaining an increasing amount of internation recognition. Would you say that Belgian cinema is in good shape?

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: When I look back at when we started out, making our documentaries, I get the impression there’s more going on now. More richness. I’m not talking about financial wealth – I’m talking about the richness of films, of the variety of films available compared to 40 or 50 years ago. There’s certainly a wealth of filmmakers, including those whose names you’ve just mentioned. There are others too. And not just in fiction, but in documentary as well, which has always been an important movement in our cinema. Because, in Belgium, we had limited resources, and the documentary genre allows you to work with fewer resources. In that respect, I’d say it’s doing well, but it’s also a victim, like everyone else in European cinema, of the financial difficulties we face.

We’re lucky here to be close to France… And most of our films – even Dutch films – are largely produced in collaboration with the French film industry. All of us in Europe are incredibly fortunate to have the ‘cultural exception’ – which was championed by France. That is why it is also important that Europe awards prizes to filmmakers. If Europe were ever to decide to abolish the ‘cultural exception’ and treat culture as just another commercial product, it would be a real disaster. Our safeguard is really the cultural exception. It is this that still allows European cinema to exist today in all its diversity and richness.

Granted, but there are threats in France too. We’re seeing this with Vincent Bolloré and Canal+, who say they’re going to cut back on their support for the film industry. These budget cuts will, of course, have an impact on French film production. It feels as though cinema is at risk of losing its importance in society and that culture is increasingly becoming a commodity to be consumed – or worse, neglected.

Luc Dardenne: We have championed the cultural exception alongside Michel Hazanavicius and other French filmmakers, as well as German and Finnish directors... We’d already noticed that the commissioners responsible for cinema, industry, the economy would say to us: ‘Is it really a good idea to keep defending this cultural exception?’ There was Borgen, the series… ‘Look, the Danes have translated it into every language and everyone loves it. And it was done in Denmark. Tomorrow, it’ll be done elsewhere. Do we still need to defend individuals, filmmakers who create unique works? We’re moving towards a cinema of TV series', and so on... We fought against that.

We’ve got nothing against TV series – there are some very good ones, including the one I just mentioned, for that matter. But we said, ‘Ladies and gentlemen, you must understand that the film industry is about jobs.' There are economic considerations to think of and it’s important to talk about that. It’s also about perspective, shared by millions of Europeans, and others too. It’s millions of people who are watching a unique work. And when they come out of a cinema, after they’ve seen a film, people talk amongst themselves. They’ve seen the film, then they re-watch it whilst discussing it, and that sparks debate. It’s a public debate and that's part of democracy. Someone is offering you a vision of the world, of reality. Whether it’s a science-fiction or a realistic one, you talk about it. It’s an invitation to debate that they’re giving you.

If we abandon cultural exception, we’ll end up with a system dictated by profit. We’ll end up with the lowest common denominator, and we’ll have no more individuality. Let individuality exist! Give us the money, for goodness’ sake! Do your jobs as Europe’s political representatives! They need to remember that culture isn’t just another commodity. People think, reflect, are moved – and their emotion is thought.

Emotion is thought...

Luc Dardenne: People tend to forget that. It isn’t something we experience and then forget. No, it stays with us. We’ve all been moved by a scene in a film… And if these scenes all end up looking the same, we won’t be moved by them anymore. It’ll pass, we’ll consume them, then forget them straight away. I hope we really do hold on to this. Here, as my brother said, is where Europe has a major role to play. Maybe this award they're giving us is a way of saying: ‘Here are two unique individuals making unique films. This must continue.’

We watch a film, we talk, we discuss, and that gets people talking about society. So cinema contributes to the debate that, I hope, brings about change and moves things forward. 

Are there any recent films that have stood out and made an impression?

Luc Dardenne: La Gradiva. That’s a very good French-Italian film by Marine Atlan. It’s a beautiful film that made an impression on both of us. We saw it a few days apart. But you see, there are two of us – my brother saw the film in Liège, I saw it in Brussels. We ring each other up and talk about the film. You can multiply that by hundreds of thousands of people. We watch a film, we talk, we discuss, and that gets people talking about society. So cinema contributes to the debate that, I hope, brings about change and moves things forward.

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: It’s the lastest one we’ve seen and I think it’s one of the greats. It’s one of the films which has moved me the most recently. And it’s a fine example of a film that’s truly alive.

Luc Dardenne: She worked, she edited, she researched, she slept poorly, she suffered… And then she was happy because she found a solution… That’s what art is all about. It’s not always pleasurable, far from it. Things don’t go to plan. We fail. We start again. And blimey, we’ve messed it up! What do we do? We’ll try to re-edit… We search and we find things. It’s marvellous. It remains a marvellous profession.

There's this excessive drive to succeed... We get it. Nobody wants to fail. But this obsession with success and recognition is terrible.

What advice would you give to young filmmakers who want to get started in this marvellous profession, as you put it?

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: You need to be around other people. You need to have friends. These days, you can make films with groups of friends, and with a mobile phone. Get going and try things out. Watching films is good too - and I’d recommend to go see the film we’ve just been talking about… To see how a young female director today manages to retain that uniqueness, that richness and that freedom. Because it’s not easy, we know that full well, and you have to fight your way through. Then there's this excessive drive to succeed... We get it. Nobody wants to fail. But this obsession with success and recognition is terrible. Here, with La Gradiva, we see that amidst all that, there’s this woman who succeeds, who really brings something to the table. It’s not just another film.

Your latest film, Jeunes mères, was screened in Cannes last year and won the award for best screenplay. If I’m not mistaken, that’s your sixth award on the Croisette. Where do you keep them all?

Luc Dardenne: (Laughs) There weren’t as many awards in the past – there used to be certificates, scrolls of paper… We’ve had two Palmes d’Or, and then, it’s true, there are other awards for screenplays, for directing… They’re in the producer’s office!

**So it's not a timeshare / "three in one household, three in another" deal? **

Luc Dardenne: (Laughs) No, not yet!

Can you tell me about your next project?

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: If things go as we’d like them to, we’re hoping to start filming next year… In September or October. That’s all I can tell you, but we’re not at all certain at the moment, given that we have zero euros.

It’s excellent that young people in France and in Belgium are making concrete demands. It’s not just about being against this or that... They’re asking for concrete things that a democratic state should normally be able to provide.

Given what is happening in France, Italy and Belgium – I'm referring to student protests and demonstrations against the high cost of living... Considering your films, which deal with everyday life and survival in a society that exacerbates everyday problems, do these social movements serve as a source of inspiration?

Luc Dardenne: The script for our next film was finished before these events took place, so I can’t say they served as a source of inspiration. But the calls for greater justice help us a great deal. We draw a great deal of inspiration from reality, from these struggles, which are sometimes individual, unknown, even almost clandestine, if I may say so. So, naturally, we’re interested in them. And it’s excellent that young people in France and in Belgium are making concrete demands. It’s not just about being against this or that... They’re asking for concrete things that a democratic state should normally be able to provide. Education is a common good. This common good must exist, and it must exist in the finest possible way in a democratic society. There is a real problem, and it’s not just in France – it’s everywhere. Let’s not even mention the United States! 

Social rights are, thankfully, being highlighted today - namely the right to food, to education, to healthcare. That's why the Democrats in the United States won. It’s because people remembered that social justice and economic justice do exist, and that they are fed up with living on the equivalent of €1,500 a month… A family with two children, who have to find a way to send them to school, put food on the table, go for a walk, take a holiday – it’s no longer possible. And people sense this, and they think: ‘They’re taking the piss, they’re no longer interested in us, they don’t care about us.’ Our films, whilst not being activist or political, etc., have always featured characters trapped in an economic and social situation linked to poverty and material hardship. That, for us, is very important. And the film we’re going to make is still part of that tradition, if I may say so. It’s about people who find themselves in a difficult situation that traps them, and they’re fighting to break free from it.

Empathy is what art is all about. (...) A work of art creates bonds.

Finally, I recently had the pleasure of attending this year’s Lumière Festival, which honoured the Coen brothers. They work together but also separately. What about you? Are you or have you ever been tempted to go your separate ways for a while?

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: (Laughs) Clearly not so far! I don’t know what’s always going on inside my brother’s head… For me, it’s never crossed my mind. In 20 or 30 years’ time, perhaps! (Laughs)

Luc Dardenne: With all due respect to the Coen brothers, I think they’re better as a pair!

I must admit, I rather agree with you...

Luc Dardenne: (Laughs) They’re going to work together again, I suppose?

I understand they’re going to do something together again.

Jean-Pierre Dardenne: Great. I must say that it’s more relaxed when it's the two of us! (Laughs) More relaxed, in the best sense of the word. We talk, we exchange ideas, and if you’ve been doing that all your life and then at some point you go your separate ways… I don’t know many filmmaking couples who’ve had the same kind of solo careers as they did when they were together. If we work together, it’s not down to chance. There’s also a sort of chemistry… As the saying goes, one plus one equals three! (Laughs)

Luc Dardenne: After working together for 40 years, we'd feel alone if we were to separate, as if a part of ourselves were cut off.

It's the samething with bands. When they split up, there's always this wish that they'd get back together... As you say, one plus one equals three…

Luc Dardenne: To go back to the start of the interview and what you called empathy... Empathy is what art is all about. In fact, even behind the camera, we always work with the same team. We love working with the same people we’ve gotten to know over the course of about fifteen films! A work of art creates bonds.

The Dardenne brothers will receive their EFA Lifetime Achievement honour at the European Film Awards on 16 January 2027 in Athens.

E-commerce giant Amazon will invest $7 billion (€6.3bn) in renewable energy projects in India. It will buy some of the electricity generated to power its operations, such as data centres.

The money will help India to reach its target of 500 gigawatts of clean energy capacity by the end of the decade, a goal the government estimates will require around $220 billion (€200bn) in investment. Coal and oil remain central to India's energy mix, with 54 per cent of the country's electricity currently coming from non-fossil fuel sources, including solar, wind and hydropower.

"Our renewable energy investments in India reflect years of sustained effort, planning, and collaboration across the industry," says Kara Hurst, Amazon's chief sustainability officer.

In 2022, Amazon emitted 51.17 million metric tonnes of CO2e – more than the likes of Switzerland, Hong Kong, and Denmark.

In 2025, Amazon's absolute carbon emissions increased by 16 per cent, mostly due to increased use of AI and data centres. In the same year, Google's emissions increased by 18 per cent and Microsoft's emissions jumped 25 per cent.

How is Amazon trying to cut its emissions?

The investments, to be made by 2030, will contribute to the Amazon's goal to reduce the carbon intensity of the electricity powering its operations by 65 per cent by 2030.

The new target means that every unit of electricity the company consumes will be associated with 65 per cent fewer carbon emissions compared to a 2019 baseline. This is part of Amazon’s Climate Pledge goal to be net-zero carbon by 2040.

Amazon's transportation emissions have accelerated at an average of 18 per cent per year since it introduced its Climate Pledge in 2019, according to the Guardian newspaper.

Amazon is one of India's top corporate buyers of renewable energy

The pledge comes on top of $4 billion (€3.3bn) in renewable energy investments Amazon has already pledged in India, making it one of the country's leading corporate purchasers of carbon-free electricity, the firm said in a statement on Tuesday.

Once operational, Amazon's contracted renewable energy projects in India will have a combined capacity of more than 2 gigawatts (GW), enough to generate electricity equivalent to the annual needs of more than 3.5 million Indian households.

Amazon is such an energy intensive company because: "Its business ventures produce massive volumes of packaging waste, emit many carbon emissions via shipping and logistics, and utilize large volumes of energy to equip its worldwide network of data centers," according to a study by Carolina Lisboa Sisnando in the Journal Of Humanities and Social Science published in 2025.

What are Amazon's solar and wind projects in India?

Amazon also announced four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined total capacity of 934 megawatts (MW). They include a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka, Amazon’s largest wind project contracted in Asia to date; a 200 MW combined solar and wind project also in Karnataka; a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh; and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan.

Un bărbat născut în România poate să trăiască, în medie, 72,8 ani. O femeie, 80,3 ani. Diferența de 7,5 ani este una dintre cele mai mari din Uniunea Europeană și depășește cu peste doi ani media europeană, de 5,2 ani, potrivit datelor Eurostat din 2024.

O parte din explicație ține de stilul de viață. O alta, de felul în care mulți bărbați se raportează la propria sănătate: controlul medical ajunge pe lista de priorități abia atunci când apare o problemă evidentă. Cât timp „nu doare nimic”, programarea la medic se amână de la un an la altul.

În noiembrie, lună dedicată la nivel internațional sănătății bărbaților, REGINA MARIA aduce prevenția într-un teritoriu în care mulți bărbați se simt ca acasă: lumea auto și oferă un pachet de analize la doar 199 lei, dedicat lor. Prin campania „Revizia anuală a bărbatului”, lansată în parteneriat cu service-ul auto Coasta de Est, bărbații sunt încurajați să acorde propriei sănătăți măcar atenția pe care o acordă mașinii: o verificare la timp, o dată pe an.

Problemele care nu aprind niciun martor în bord 

Cancerul de prostată este unul dintre cele mai frecvente cancere la bărbații din România. Potrivit GLOBOCAN, în 2022 au fost înregistrate 10.442 de cazuri noi, adică 18,2% din toate cancerele diagnosticate la bărbați. În stadiile incipiente, boala poate evolua fără niciun simptom.

„Cele mai multe afecțiuni ale prostatei, inclusiv cancerul, nu dau semne la început. Mulți bărbați ajung la urolog abia când apar simptomele: se trezesc tot mai des noaptea să meargă la baie, jetul urinar slăbește sau apare o durere. Un control făcut atunci când te simți bine îți dă șansa să descoperi o problemă înainte să devină complicată”, explică dr. Bogdan Sandu, medic specialist urologie la REGINA MARIA.

Bărbații au specificații și nevoi diferite, la fel ca mașinile 

Campania pornește de la o comparație familiară: la fel ca mașinile, bărbații au „specificații” diferite, în funcție de genetică și stil de viață, și vulnerabilități care merită verificate mai des.

Ideea prinde viață într-o serie de filme construite după logica prezentărilor auto, în care publicul face cunoștință cu cinci „modele”: Victor V6, Radu Turbo Diesel, Adrian GT, Mihnea RS și Ioan Coupe, tipologii de bărbați prezentate cu umor, cu an de fabricație, tip de motor și posibile vulnerabilități. Fiecare model pornește de la un tip de pacient pe care medicii îl întâlnesc des în cabinet. Victor V6 e plin de energie și convins că e pe cai mari: are destui cai putere cât să creadă că nimic nu-l poate opri. Adrian GT pornește la prima cafea și ajunge de la zero la 100 de idei pe oră în 8 secunde. Mihnea RS adună kilometri pe traseul școală–birou–supermarket, fără nicio oprire la boxe, până când motorul începe să dea rateuri. Ioan Coupe e un model de croazieră, cu opriri frecvente la vernisaje.

Chiar și cel mai fiabil model are nevoie de o revizie, iar cel mai bun moment pentru ea este atunci când totul pare să funcționeze bine.

Ce include „revizia”

Pachetul de analize „Revizia anuală a bărbatului” este disponibil bărbaților la costul de 199, până pe 31 decembrie în policlinicile și punctele de recoltare ale rețelei. Pachetul verifică funcția rinichilor și a ficatului, metabolismul (glicemia și acidul uric), profilul lipidic, hemoleucograma completă și fierul seric, tiroida (TSH), precum și doi indicatori dedicați sănătății bărbatului: testosteronul și PSA-ul.

Pentru pachet este nevoie de o programare în call center, la 021 9268, și de o singură vizită pentru recoltare. Rezultatele apar direct în aplicația REGINA MARIA. Filmele campaniei pot fi urmărite pe www.reginamaria.ro/revizia-anuala.
