From smoky-flavoured snacks to ketchup sachets, ministers are pushing back against claims that closer ties with Brussels will mean a new wave of EU rules for British consumers.

Smoky bacon crisps are safe, marmalade is staying put, and the United Kingdom won't have to ditch its ketchup sachets.

As Brexit tensions resurface ahead of a crunch UK-EU summit, the government is scrambling to quash claims that closer ties with Brussels could mean a fresh wave of European rules for British consumers.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s team has released a "factsheet and mythbuster" document, which it hopes will clarify "several points" about a package being negotiated with the European Union.

The summit, set to be held in Brussels on Friday, will focus on three specific agreements – cutting red tape for food exports, linking the two sides' emissions-trading schemes and finalising a "youth experience" scheme.

The UK government hopes the food and drinks deal alone could add some £5.1 billion (€6.12 billion) to the country's economy.

As Burnham’s government makes moves to get closer to the EU in a post-Brexit world, some parts of the UK media have been pushing a narrative which suggests this relationship could usher in a new era of EU influence on Britain.

"Smoky flavours in crisps, sauces, and soups will remain on UK supermarket shelves," the statement put out by the government said.

It also added that "British marmalade will not need to be relabelled, as most British marmalade brands on supermarket shelves already meet European labelling rules.”

The statement also makes it clear that a ban on small sachets of ketchup and mayonnaise or on single-use plastics, including straws, cutlery and cotton buds, will not feature as part of the draft agreements on the table.

Burnham’s detractors worry Brexit could be reversed

Despite Burnham’s keenness to forge a closer relationship with the bloc, many pro-Brexit campaigners fear he’ll soon push to rejoin the EU.

In 2016, a tiny majority voted to leave the 27-nation alliance, many for the supposed financial drain the EU had on the UK.

To quell some of that fear, Burnham’s statement also dismissed "largely speculative" reports that the UK would have to pay millions of pounds into the EU budget under the new package.

The Prime Minister has also committed to his predecessor, Keir Starmer's "red lines" on Europe for this parliament – that means there will be no return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

Speaking this week, Burnham said discussions about the long-term relationship with the EU beyond the next election – due by 2029 at the latest – would only begin after Friday's summit.

"The deal that's on the table will bring growth to the British economy," he said, “The truth is the Brexit deal that they negotiated wasn't good enough," he said.

"They've burned bridges with our largest market, old friends and neighbours. They just destroyed all of those relationships,” Burnham added.

The Spanish National High Court has admitted a complaint filed by two former employees of Julio Iglesias alleging sexual offences, bodily harm and degrading treatment. The singer has been summoned to testify on 3 February.

A Spanish court opened an investigation into veteran singer Julio Iglesias on Wednesday after two former employees filed a complaint alleging sexual abuse, which he denies.

Madrid's Audiencia Nacional court said in a statement that it would investigate alleged "offences against sexual freedom", a category covering a range of crimes, including sexual assault, as well as bodily harm and degrading treatment.

The decision marks a reversal after an earlier complaint was dismissed on the grounds that Spanish courts lacked jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic.

The women, a domestic worker and a physiotherapist, allege they were subjected to sexual abuse and other forms of mistreatment while working at Iglesias' properties in the two Caribbean countries in 2021.

Judge finds sufficient grounds for investigation

Following the dismissal of the complaint, Women’s Link Worldwide announced last September that it would take the case directly to the National High Court by filing a criminal complaint against the singer.

The organisation accused him of alleged offences of human trafficking for the purposes of forced labour and servitude, offences against sexual freedom and sexual integrity, bodily harm, degrading treatment and violations of workers' rights through the imposition of abusive working conditions.

Antonio Piña, a judge at Spain’s National High Court, has partially admitted the complaint: he will investigate the alleged offences against sexual freedom, bodily harm and degrading treatment, but has excluded human trafficking and offences against workers' rights.

The judge considers that there is sufficient evidence to open criminal proceedings. In his ruling, he highlights that, in addition to the witness statements, the prosecution has submitted a photograph of one of the employees "showing a bruise on one of her arms, consistent with the possibility of having been grabbed forcefully".

In the same image, the investigating judge adds, "two marks can be seen on one of her thighs which may correspond to a bite mark from another person". According to the complaint, these injuries "are the result of her being forced to participate in acts of a sexual nature".

Iglesias, 83, a Grammy-winning singer who has sold more than 300 million records over his decades-long career, has described the accusations as "absolutely false", saying he has never "abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman".

A court in Iraq on Wednesday sentenced six French citizens, among them the jihadist , to life in prison for belonging to the Islamic State (IS) group.

The six are among 47 French nationals who were transferred from Syria to Iraq last year and charged with membership of the extremist organisation. Their trials began in September. Ten of the group had already been sentenced, most of them to life imprisonment, before Wednesday’s verdicts, which were reported by an AFP journalist in the courtroom.

Barnouin, 45, told the court during his trial this month that he went to Syria because he believed it was his religious duty. He said he had not known that IS would go on to carry out attacks in France.

A convert to Islam in the early 2000s, he was gradually radicalised and became part of a jihadist network in southwestern France. The network included Mohamed Merah, who killed four people, three of them children, at a Jewish school in Toulouse, France, in 2012.

Barnouin joined IS in Syria in 2014. Three years later, Kurdish-led forces captured him.

Overcrowded prisons

Iraq’s jails were already holding large numbers of suspected jihadists when, in February, the United States moved more than 5,700 IS detainees from over 60 countries into Iraqi custody. They had spent years in prisons in Syria run by Kurdish-led forces. A court source said their trials would begin on Sunday.

Iraqi courts have issued hundreds of death sentences and life terms over the years to people convicted of terrorism, including foreign fighters. Some human rights groups have criticised the proceedings as hasty and say defendants are denied due process.

At its height, between 2014 and 2017, IS controlled swathes of territory across Iraq and Syria. During that time it carried out massacres and forced women and girls into sexual slavery.

Baghdad declared victory over the group in 2017 with the support of a US-led coalition. Two years later, Kurdish-led forces backed by Washington defeated IS in Syria. Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan have drawn up a joint plan to increase Middle Corridor freight capacity to around 30 million tonnes a year by 2029, as Belgian companies discuss a logistics hub in Kazakhstan and digital upgrades to the Asia-Europe trade route.

Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan are stepping up cooperation to develop the Middle Corridor, an emerging trade route connecting China and Central Asia with European markets via the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus to the Black Sea.

The three countries have developed a joint plan aimed at improving transport infrastructure, streamlining logistics, and making cross-border trade faster and more efficient.

The joint plan comes as European companies explore new investment opportunities along the route, including a proposed $50 million (€45.4mn) logistics hub in Kazakhstan and a digital project aimed at reducing delays at border crossings.

Together, the initiatives reflect growing efforts to make the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, commonly known as the Middle Corridor, a more efficient and competitive connection between Asia and Europe.

The Iran war has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, increasing the value of alternative trade routes for moving goods between Asia and Europe.

Belgian companies explore major logistics investment

European businesses are also examining opportunities to participate in the build-up of the corridor’s infrastructure and operations.

During a working visit to Brussels on 16 November, Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi met with senior executives from Belgian companies Sarens Group, Ahlers Logistics, and BIM e-Solutions to discuss investment, logistics and digital technology.

According to Kazakhstan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, talks with Sarens Group Senior Advisor Hendrik Sarens and Matthias Sarens, Construction Director of the Transport and Logistics Centre at the Khorgos Customs & Logistics Platform, included the proposed $50mn (€45.4mn) investment in Kazakhstan's Zhetysu Region, near the Chinese border.

The planned transport and logistics hub would include a 2.1-kilometre bypass road, temporary storage facilities, and specialised infrastructure for handling heavy cargo.

If implemented, the hub is expected to increase capacity at the Nur Zholy border crossing, which is one of the gateways for goods entering Kazakhstan from China, and relieve freight congestion along the Kazakh-Chinese border.

Reducing congestion at this crossing could help improve the movement of freight entering the wider Middle Corridor network.

A target of 30 million tonnes a year by 2029

In Georgia, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Sustainable Development Mariam Kvrivishvili confirmed the joint plan in an interview with Georgia's Imedi TV.

She said Georgia was working "very closely with partner countries", "particularly Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan", to improve transport links and increase the volume of cargo moving through the corridor.

"This plan aims to ensure the transportation of 30 million tonnes of cargo through the Middle Corridor by 2029. We are working in constant cooperation with our partners and have identified joint regional measures," Kvrivishvili said.

Reaching that target will require improvements across a transport network involving railways, ports, shipping services and border crossings.

Kvrivishvili said Georgia plans to invest approximately $7 billion (€6.4bn) in transport infrastructure by 2029, covering ports, railways, roads and aviation infrastructure.

The joint measures focus on harmonising customs clearance, aligning tariff policies, and expanding port and rail capacity across the Caspian and South Caucasus segments.

Regional analysts note that hitting this ambitious volume target could fundamentally shift how international shippers view the route.

"The Middle Corridor has grown in strategic importance, but limited freight capacity remains one of its biggest constraints," said Bako Kheladze, a research fellow at the Turan Research Centre.

Kheladze pointed out that while the World Bank estimated in 2023 that the route could triple its freight volume by 2030 and cut transit times in half with the right investment and policies, it still operates on a much smaller scale than the Northern Route through Russia.

"If the three countries can reach that target and offer reliable transit times, the Middle Corridor could become a regular route for shippers between Asia and Europe. The Northern Route would still have an advantage in scale, but the Middle Corridor could compete for a meaningful share of freight even if transit through Russia becomes easier again," he added.

Cross-regional connectivity

Meanwhile, in Brussels on Monday, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos and International Partnerships Commissioner Jozef Síkela met with foreign ministers and other senior representatives of EU member states, the Republic of Moldova, Turkey, Ukraine, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan at the second Ministerial Meeting on Cross-Regional Security and Connectivity.

The parties noted the role of connectivity in maintaining economic resilience and sustainable growth.

Mukhtar Tileuberdi, Kazakh Minister of Foreign Affairs, emphasised that developing the country’s transport and transit links and modernising its infrastructure are among its strategic priorities.

“Kazakhstan is interested in further development of this transport route in cooperation with European and regional partners. This involves increasing infrastructure capacity, improving logistics processes, and creating a more efficient cargo delivery system,” he said.

Tileuberdi added that this ambition highlights the importance of the Global Gateway initiative, in particular in attracting investment, developing transport infrastructure, and implementing joint projects.

Could digital technology speed up trade?

Infrastructure is only part of the challenge.

Moving freight efficiently across several countries also depends on customs procedures, documentation, and the exchange of information between transport operators.

Separate discussions with Ahlers Logistics CEO Dave van den Bos and BIM e-Solutions head Michael Barrie covered how to integrate software along the route, including a proposal for a 90-day Digital Middle Corridor pilot project.

The proposed trial would introduce end-to-end digital freight tracking and streamline cross-border customs data exchange to help reduce transit delays.

For European businesses, more reliable transit times and simpler border procedures could make the corridor more attractive for transporting goods between Asia and Europe.

The latest developments come as the European Union seeks to strengthen transport connections with Central Asia and the South Caucasus.

Born without arms near the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site, Karipbek Kuyukov became an artist and anti-nuclear activist. Today, he continues to campaign against nuclear weapons through his art and public appearances.

In his apartment, behind a door marked "Art Studio", Kazakh artist Karipbek Kuyukov is working on a painting. He leans close to the canvas, holding a brush in his mouth. Every now and then, he rolls his chair back to look at the painting from a distance before moving closer again. He is painting a landscape. Autumn leaves cover a road leading towards mountains rising in the distance.

“I love painting landscapes. I want to show that wherever humans appear, they end up spoiling nature,” he says.

The mountains in his painting are Balkantau, near the village of Yegindybulak, about 100 kilometres from the former Semipalatinsk nuclear test site.

It is in this village that Kuyukov was born, without arms.

"When I was born, they showed me to my mother, and she saw that I had no arms. It was very difficult for her," he recalls.

Between 1949 and 1989, the Soviet Union conducted 456 nuclear tests at Semipalatinsk.

Kuyukov remembers the ground shaking after explosions, with shockwaves spreading like ripples in water. He recalls that many other children in the area were also born with disabilities.

Growing up, Kuyukov learned to use his feet instead of hands. One day, he came across a large box of coloured pencils and began experimenting with drawing. He started making simple childhood sketches, using his feet to hold the pencils.

Activism through art

In 1989, Kazakh poet and activist Olzhas Suleimenov founded the Nevada–Semipalatinsk anti-nuclear movement, which Kuyukov later joined. He took part in the movement's activities, but it was through his paintings that he found a powerful way to express his message.

His first painting on the subject, titled "The First Explosion", depicted a family inside a yurt caught in the force of a nuclear blast.

"The blast blows the yurt away, turning everything upside down. I wanted to show what the people living there went through and how the nuclear tests affected them," he explains.

He went on to create more works exploring the impact of nuclear testing, including "Nuclear Mushroom", "Atomic Childhood", "Radiation" and "Fear".

This year marks 35 years since the closure of the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site in 1991. Kuyukov was invited to address a high-level meeting of the UN General Assembly about the human cost of nuclear testing.

"I wanted to shout, not just speak, because the time has come to make the whole world hear us," he says. "I addressed the leaders of countries that continue to make nuclear threats."

It was not his first appearance at the UN. Over the years, he has continued to campaign against nuclear weapons through his paintings and public speeches.

With nuclear threats once again part of international political rhetoric, Kuyukov's decades-long campaign remains relevant.

A life in his own words

Kuyukov has recently published his first autobiography, a project he began 35 years ago and only recently completed. With financial support from people who believed in the project, he recorded his memories as voice messages, which editors then turned into a manuscript.

Recounting his life brings him to tears. His sister Saule gently wipes them from his face. He calls her his "guardian angel". In the book, he pays tribute to her and others who have supported him over the years.

At the book launch, people line up to have their copies signed. Kuyukov patiently signs each one, holding a pen in his mouth. As he grew older, he gradually lost the ability to use his feet for drawing and writing. Today, he relies on his mouth for both.

Beyond the canvas

Back in his apartment, Kuyukov takes a break for tea. On the table is a specially designed stand. Saule places a bowl of tea on it, bringing it up to the level of his chin. He drinks without assistance.

Saule is often by his side, although she prefers not to be interviewed.

Later, sitting on the sofa in his living room, Kuyukov tucks one leg beneath him as he talks. His other foot moves in rhythm with his speech, gesturing almost as hands would.

Today, he increasingly turns to landscapes, painting mountains and scenes of nature untouched by humans. But his commitment to a world free of nuclear weapons remains unchanged. He continues to share his story through his art and public appearances.

Despite decades of painting, there is one person Kuyukov has never dared to portray: his mother. He says he is afraid to paint her portrait, but hopes that one day he will find the courage to do so.

Before the Brussels performance, Euronews Culture spoke to Gergely Barcza, one of Besh o droM's founders.

"The audience should get ready for a really big party," said Barcza. "Over the past 27 years, Besh o droM has always built on partying, dancing and a great atmosphere, and that has worked very well. Bohemian Betyars bring a very similar energy."

Easy access to dubious health tests should be considered a “patient safety issue,” researchers said.

You can find tests to screen for dozens of health conditions online — but many of them make baseless and potentially harmful claims, a new analysis has found.

Researchers in the United Kingdom analysed 50 health tests that were advertised online, including tests for the gut microbiome, blood counts, genetics, liver and lung function and cortisol levels, as well as pelvic and breast examinations, chest X-rays and ultrasounds.

Advertisers were both online retailers and in-person clinics. Prices ranged from £6.99 (€8.36) for an at-home “kidney albumin rapid test” to £14,000 (€16,751) for a “platinum assessment” that offered multiple tests, imaging and a physical exam. Some clinics offered a luxury hotel or spa package on top, with celebrities or influencers offering endorsements for other tests.

Yet many of these tests made unsubstantiated claims or offered screening that is not recommended by national health authorities, according to the study, which was published in the journal BMJ Open.

Sixteen tests claimed, without evidence, that they could help people live longer, while 36 promised earlier diagnosis and better health outcomes. Only 15 tests explained the potential downsides of testing, such as inaccuracy or risks from intimate physical exams.

In one example, a retailer cited death rates from a particular disease, saying they “could have been detected by one of our … health assessments. Just think of how many could still be here today”.

Among the 50 vendors in the study, 14 offered testicular exams, 13 offered breast exams and nine offered pelvic exams to people without worrisome symptoms. The UK’s national health system does not recommend these tests for everyone.

Consumer health tests are easy to access, with few regulatory guardrails, “despite their capability of harm,” wrote the researchers from the University of St Andrews in Scotland.

They said at-home health tests can help fill gaps in the medical system, but only if they are evidence-backed. Poor-quality screenings, they warned, can result in “false positives (false alarms), false negatives (false reassurance) and loss of personal resources with little or no value gained by individuals.”

At-home health tests are easy to find online. On Wednesday, the UK’s Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) upheld a ban on advertisements for an at-home testosterone blood test from Voy, an online provider that sells testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.

The watchdog said Voy’s ads were “misleading” because they linked common symptoms, such as fatigue and irritability, to low testosterone to encourage men to buy a test kit.

Voy argued that the ads did not claim that low testosterone was the only explanation for those symptoms, according to the ASA. But the watchdog decided against the company anyway, ordering Voy not to “exaggerate” the connection.

Few cases make it to regulators, the new study found. “This should be considered a gap in regulation and a patient safety issue,” the researchers said.

Setting up a small business in Germany takes almost 4,000 hours of red tape, the equivalent of nearly 500 eight-hour working days. That is the longest among 27 countries across Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, and nearly 18 times as long as in France, which ranked first in a new study.

Germany is the slowest place to open a small business among 27 countries in Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, with entrepreneurs needing 3,942 hours, or almost 500 eight-hour working days, to get through the red tape.

That is nearly 18 times as long as in France, which tops the ranking of the Index of Bureaucracy 2026.

The index, compiled by the Adam Smith Center for Economic Freedom at Florida International University in Miami, counts the hours a small company needs to get through the procedures required to start operating legally, from registering the firm to obtaining local permits, including waiting for approvals.

It is not an EU-wide ranking, as the study covers 27 countries, including 20 in Latin America and the Caribbean, five in the EU, namely France, Germany, Italy, Portugal and Spain, as well as the UK and Ukraine.

The average across all 27 is 1,638 hours, the equivalent of about nine and a half months of eight-hour working days.

The centre, created by the state of Florida in 2020, describes itself as an independent, non-partisan think tank that aims to advance economic freedom.

This edition was backed by the Templeton World Charity Foundation, a philanthropy set up by the late investor Sir John Templeton, while data for Germany were gathered with the Berlin Center for Individualist Thought, a group promoting free-market ideas.

The report's lead author, Sary Levy-Carciente, is an economist and senior research scientist at the centre who coordinates the index, and spoke to Euronews.

Slower than Venezuela

Germany, the EU's largest economy, comes last in the ranking, behind every Latin American and Caribbean country in the study, including Venezuela at 2,738 hours and Peru, the second-slowest, at 3,853 hours.

Its total is more than double the average.

Valued at Germany's average wage of $31 (€28) an hour, the rate used in the report, those hours would be worth about $122,000 (€110,890), against roughly $4,200 (€3,817) in France, where the average wage is $19 (€17) an hour.

Municipal permits and registration account for about 2,400 of Germany's hours, and identification and registry steps for about 1,440, according to index data shared with Euronews.

"Germany's bureaucratic burden is heavily front-loaded by complex local requirements," Levy-Carciente explained to Euronews, adding that "local trade offices interact with numerous independent municipal departments, each requiring distinct physical paperwork or sequential approvals."

"Mandatory notarisation for corporate forms combined with electronic processing backlogs at local courts adds substantial waiting time," she said.

Germany's figure is an average of three sample businesses, weighted by their sectors' share of the economy. A pig and grain farm or a machine-tool maker needs 8,633 hours, the data show, including the time needed to obtain a full environmental permit under Germany's pollution control law, while a car dealership and repair shop needs 2,056 hours.

The findings come as Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government tries to cut red tape to revive the economy. His coalition agreement pledged in 2025 to create a digital one-stop shop that would let companies be set up within 24 hours.

In June, more than 100 founders and managers backed an appeal by the German Startup Association, which lobbies for young companies, calling for businesses to be able to register within 24 hours anywhere in the country.

For comparison, at the top of the index, France needs just 223 hours, or about 28 working days. Italy is second at 303 hours and Portugal fourth at 335, just behind Brazil, while Spain needs 707 hours, more than twice as long as neighbouring Portugal.

All four are well below the average, as is Ukraine at 603 hours, while the UK, at 1,873 hours, sits above it.

Asked what the fastest countries get right, Levy-Carciente pointed to the figures for municipal permits and registration.

Those steps take about an hour in France and 24 hours in Italy, against some 2,400 in Germany, the same data show.

Not a question of wealth

The report finds no link between the time it takes to open a business and a country's income or level of development, pointing instead to each government's commitment to running an efficient administration.

Across the 27 countries, procedures specific to a company's line of business are the biggest hurdle, averaging 706 hours, or 43% of the total, followed by municipal permits at 515 hours.

Excessive red tape discourages entrepreneurs from starting companies and pushes some into the informal economy, the report warns. It also cautions that going digital is not enough on its own, as poorly designed systems risk "automating inefficiency".

Brussels is trying to speed things up.

In March, the European Commission proposed an optional EU-wide company form, dubbed EU Inc, that would let entrepreneurs register a business within 48 hours, fully online and for up to €100.

The Estado Novo Interpretive Centre occupies a former primary school in the town where the Portuguese dictator was born and is dedicated to studying the regime and resistance movements.

After two decades of stop-start progress and controversy, the former Salazar School-Canteen in Vimieiro, where dictator António de Oliveira Salazar was born, has been turned into the Estado Novo Interpretive Centre - Regime and Resistance (CIEN - RR).

The former primary school in the municipality of Santa Comba Dão, built between 1937 and 1940, reopened on 23 October to tell the story of the Estado Novo, censorship and resistance to the dictatorship.

The venue is under the scientific coordination of the Associação Ephemera, founded by historian José Pacheco Pereira, whose aim is to collect and disseminate collections, archives, books, periodicals, manuscripts, pamphlets, photos and objects from contemporary history.

The interpretive centre will host exhibitions, debates, conferences and research activities, as well as a thematic library and a reading room. The aim is to provide documents and materials that help to understand life under the Estado Novo, without hiding the building's historical link to Salazar.

The old school still retains elements associated with that era. For those responsible for the project, preserving this context is part of the work of historical interpretation, rather than turning it into a tribute.

The first exhibition, entitled "Only What Is Known To Exist Exists: Censorship under the Estado Novo", which brings together material from the Ephemera association's collection, looks at the mechanisms for controlling information and cultural expression during the dictatorship, including the press, literature and music.

At the formal opening session, the Secretary of State for Culture, Alberto Santos, argued, according to the Lusa news agency, that "studying the dictatorship is a responsibility of democracy".

According to the remarks by the Secretary of State quoted by Lusa, studying the dictatorship "in a place so directly associated with the figure of António de Oliveira Salazar", the central figure of the Estado Novo, increases the responsibility "to know the regime, to understand how it managed to last for so long, what it meant to live under its power" and what lesson it left for the future.

The opening of the centre brings to a close a process that spanned different municipal terms of office and generated debate on how to address the memory of Salazar in his home town. The new venue now seeks to establish itself as a place of historical knowledge and reflection on the dictatorship and the resistance to it, rather than a museum dedicated to the former ruler.

"We do not want to turn this interpretive centre into a museum to the dictator, we want instead to create an interpretive centre that studies not only the regime, but also the resistance to the regime", stressed the deputy mayor of Santa Comba Dão, Luís Nunes, in comments to Lusa.

The centre's scientific committee is made up of Marçal Grilo, Irene Pimentel, José Manuel Sobral, José Pedro Castanheira, Luís Nunes, Maria Inácia Rezola, Luísa Tiago de Oliveira and Rui Feijó.

At the inauguration of the facility, historian Pacheco Pereira stressed that most of them are people who "before and after 25 April played a role in defending freedom and democracy".

Four more EU countries have joined Finland, France, Germany and the Netherlands in publishing national roadmaps for the transition away from fossil fuels.

Fossil fuels – the main drivers of global warming – remain a flashpoint at COP31 as the UN climate summit enters its final days.

Despite many leaders shying away from mentioning a transition away from coal, oil and gas during the talks, a draft deal published on Monday (16 November) called for “accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”.

After last year’s summit in Brazil ended without any mention of fossil fuels in its final agreement, countries in support of a phaseout have welcomed stronger language on the issue – but the draft is intended to ignite discussion on contentious topics.

Resistance, particularly from fossil fuel-exporting countries, is likely to feed into the final text. Agreements at the UN summit require consensus from all parties – that’s nearly 200 nations – which means progress is often slow and incremental.

'Electrification needs to be clearly linked to a transition away from fossil fuels'

Despite mounting warnings that the world will overshoot the 1.5℃ threshold, the biggest cause of planet-heating emissions – burning fossil fuels for energy – has been notably absent from some major talks at the summit.

President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, addressed leaders in Antalya on 11 November – describing the recent bout of extreme weather and deadly wildfires that wrecked Europe and the rest of the world as the “summer of truth”.

“We are at a global tipping point,” she said. “The latest UN report is clear: We’re on course to overshoot the 1.5℃ target and every fraction of a degree matters.”

Von der Leyen laid out the EU’s priorities for COP31, including accelerating electrification and “strengthening global partnerships” to build clean economies – but at no point in her speech did she mention fossil fuels.

According to the UN, fossil fuels – coal, oil and gas – are by far the largest contributor to global climate change, accounting for around 68 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions and nearly 90 per cent of all carbon dioxide emissions.

Von der Leyen was accused of “missing the mark” by not mentioning a word on transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF) and for using a “celebratory tone” despite EU climate finance flatlining.

“Electrification needs to be clearly linked to a transition away from fossil fuels, otherwise it gives the fossil fuel industry cover to carry on as usual, raking in profits while ordinary people are hit by rising energy bills and impacts,” says Chiara Martinelli, Director at Climate Action Network (CAN) Europe.

Four more EU countries launch fossil fuel phaseout roadmap

But for some, COP's closing text is not the be all and end all.

While “you can always wish and fight” for TAFF to be anchored in the cover decision, “this is not for us the ultimate benchmark for success,” German Environment Ministry State Secretary Heike Henn told reporters on Monday (16 November), ahead of the draft’s publication. “The success is in doing, in a growing coalition,” she said.

On 11 November, Finland affirmed its commitment to TAFF by publishing a national roadmap, following in the footsteps of France, Germany and the Netherlands.

Almost a week later (17 November), Denmark, Portugal, Luxembourg and Spain announced their own national plans.

After spearheading a global TAFF roadmap before handing over the COP presidency, Brazil is also actively working on its own domestic national roadmap, along with various Pacific Island Nations.

“It is positive to see more countries responding to the call to plan their future beyond fossil fuels,” says Romain Ioualalen of non-profit Oil Change International.

“However, roadmaps need to be more than just a reiteration of existing policies: we need to see rich countries accelerate their exit from fossil fuels to align with global climate goals.”

What share of Finland's energy comes from fossil fuels?

More than 96 per cent of Finland’s electricity is already generated from non-fossil sources, one of the highest shares in the world.

However, the energy intensity of the economy and energy consumption per capita are both very high due to the country’s relatively large heavy industry sector, long travel distances, and the high heating demand due to its cold climate.

In 2025 the largest individual energy source, wood fuels, accounted for 28 per cent of its total energy consumption, while nuclear and fossil fuels made up 27 and 18 per cent respectively.

The main domestic energy sources currently are wood-based fuels, hydropower, wind power, solar power, waste, peat, and heat pumps.

Finland, which aims to become carbon neutral by 2035, did not however set a legally binding deadline to TAFF. Its roadmap follows the Santa Marta process on TAFF after all mentions of establishing a fossil fuel transition roadmap were scrubbed from the final text of COP30 in Belém last year.

Fossil fuel phaseout ‘doesn’t make sense’ without financing

Türkiye, France, the US and Italy are some of the countries that have brought fossil fuel lobbyists to the annual climate summit, once again drawing scrutiny of who gets a seat at the table and the integrity of its process.

Co-host Türkiye has also garnered criticism for its heavy reliance on coal, which remains its biggest source of power.

Despite pushing to expand renewables, the country’s national climate plan also allows for an increase in its greenhouse gas emissions rather than a decrease – as it continues to step up fossil fuel exploration both in the Black Sea and in the country’s south.

In fact, as COP31 kicked off on 9 November, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan celebrated the fact that the country had made an oil discovery on its territory.

On 12 November, Türkiye’s Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar – who has previously claimed that fossil fuels are required for energy security – said that developing countries need access to technology and financing or they won’t be able to make the transition to clean energy.

"Without that, to tell the people you don’t need to consume coal, you don’t need to consume other fossil fuels, it doesn’t make any sense," he told news agency AFP.

“We need to produce this electricity. We would like to make it with renewables. We would like to make it with nuclear – but of course to develop nuclear power plants, a huge amount of finance [is] required.”

Financing has become one of the most contested issues in Antalya, particularly to fund adaptation and loss and damage in countries most vulnerable to climate disasters, like developing nations and small island states.

At COP29 in Baku in 2024, developed countries agreed to mobilise at least $300 billion (€268bn) a year for developing nations by 2035, as part of a wider $1.3 trillion (€1.63tn) target from public and private sources.

At COP30 last year, governments agreed to push for at least a tripling of adaptation finance by 2035, but without settling the baseline, who pays or how the money will be delivered.

Analysts say one “feasible route to a meaningful outcome” on climate finance at COP31 would be anchoring the tripling pledge and agreeing a $40 billion (€36.2 billion) baseline with interim milestones before 2035 – with a minimum share of grants compared with loans.

But a UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report published days before the summit found that even tripling current international public adaptation finance would only meet 23-29 per cent of developing countries’ needs.

COP31’s electrification pledge gains momentum – and criticism

The transition away from fossil fuels has become a hot topic at COP31, not least due to the spiralling costs of oil and gas following the US-led war on Iran.

Fossil fuels have also become a growing concern given Türkiye’s '35x35' pledge. This would see the global share of energy demand met by electricity increase to 35 per cent, up from around 23 per cent today, by 2035.

Some 75 countries and several small island states have now publicly backed the goal, including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham – just weeks after his government approved the controversial Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

Von der Leyen also showed support, arguing that the pledge is in reach and will provide greater energy security for the EU.

Electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels with electricity – such as going from a diesel-powered car to an electric vehicle (EV).

But critics warn that electrification in itself will not eradicate fossil fuel use and could be used as an excuse to allow governments to count expanded gas-fired generation as progress towards the 35-by-35 pledge.

“Switching from oil and gas to electricity only cuts emissions if that electricity is clean – making the rapid build-out of renewables non-negotiable,” says Linda Kalcher, executive director at pan-European think tank Strategic Perspectives

“Solar and wind are the cheapest and among the fastest sources of new electricity worldwide, even more since oil and gas prices soared. The risk of further fossil-fuel lock-in and investment in uneconomical oil and gas reserves remains though – not least as rising energy demand from data centres fuels calls for new fossil-fuel capacity.”

COP31 is due to end on 20 November, though talks may enter overtime as countries grapple to reach consensus.

This article was originally published on 14 November. It has been updated to include the draft cover decision released on 16 November and new countries announcing TAFF roadmaps on 17 November.

Hosting the UN’s land conference in Ulaanbaatar gave Mongolia an opportunity to demonstrate its organising capacity and put the future of rangelands and pastoral communities at the centre of international attention.

For Mongolia, land is inseparable from daily life. It sustains herding families, supports food production and carries a cultural inheritance shaped by generations of movement across the steppe. Bringing the world’s land conference to Ulaanbaatar gave those experiences an international platform.

From 17 to 28 August 2026, Mongolia hosted the seventeenth Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, known as UNCCD COP17. Delegates from the Convention’s 197 Parties joined representatives of business, science and civil society under the theme “Restoring Land. Restoring Hope.”

The gathering marked a milestone for the country: Mongolia became the first host of a UNCCD COP in East and Central Asia. For the government, it was an opportunity to connect the demands of organising a major multilateral conference with an issue of direct national importance. Nearly 77 per cent of Mongolia’s land is degraded, according to UNDP, placing pressure on livelihoods, ecosystems and the country’s pastoral heritage.

A national effort with international reach

Hosting a conference of this scale requires coordination across government, international organisations, local partners and the people supporting delegates throughout their stay.

The organising effort extended beyond the negotiating rooms. UNDP’s support included more than 400 UN Volunteers working alongside the National Organizing Committee, the Mongolian Red Cross and other partners across logistics, communications and delegate services. Their involvement also created opportunities to develop skills and experience that can serve future events.

Translating this high-level ambition into a seamless reality required unprecedented logistical coordination. At the core of organizing the event in Mongolia was Batbayar Shurenchuluun, State Secretary of the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change. As part of the National Organizing Committee and the primary public servant spearheading the on-the-ground execution of the conference, he united domestic agencies, NGOs, and the massive volunteer force to accommodate over 10,000 delegates—twice the number initially expected.

"Hosting a multilateral gathering of this magnitude was a profound test of our national capacity and public service," State Secretary Batbayar noted. "The extraordinary dedication of our local partners, institutions, and volunteers created the vital, stable foundation needed to facilitate the complex international negotiations that followed."

By effectively translating international dialogue into actionable frameworks, the conference yielded concrete results—securing multi-billion dollar financial pledges and establishing targeted initiatives that will drive sustainable land management and herder resilience for decades to come.

The ambition of these global initiatives mirrored Mongolia's own domestic commitments. As a National Policy Advocate during the COP17 thematic sessions, State Secretary Batbayar officially presented Mongolia's domestic conservation strategies to the international community. He detailed the country's proactive goal to build a long-term foundation for natural conservation by placing 30 per cent of its total territory under state special protection by 2030, with a further ambition to increase this to 35 per cent by 2050.

The diplomatic task was equally demanding. Governments arrived with different priorities and expectations. Mongolia’s presidency supported negotiations through high-level consultations, helping create the conditions for 34 decisions to be adopted, including on rangelands, land tenure, sand and dust storms, and resource mobilisation.

That achievement gives the hosting story substance: Ulaanbaatar provided a setting in which countries could continue working towards shared responses to land degradation despite difficult negotiations.

Bringing the world’s rangelands into focus

Mongolia’s clearest contribution was to elevate an issue rooted in its own experience.

Rangelands cover approximately 54 per cent of the world’s terrestrial surface and support around 500 million pastoralists. Their condition has implications for food production, biodiversity and the resilience of communities far beyond Mongolia.

COP17 took place during the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, an initiative championed by Mongolia. Hosting the conference brought that international recognition into a country where pastoralism remains integral to livelihoods and national identity.

The decisions adopted in Ulaanbaatar encouraged stronger policies for the sustainable management, conservation and restoration of rangelands, alongside improved tenure security. The conference also saw the launch of the Rangelands Flagship Initiative, intended to increase investment in these landscapes.

For pastoral communities, this attention matters because the future of land depends on the people who manage it. Their knowledge and experience are essential to designing responses that work locally.

Connecting ambition with investment

A lasting conference legacy also depends on the partnerships and projects it helps advance.

In its closing assessment, the Mongolian government highlighted a portfolio of 45 land restoration, rangeland and drought-resilience projects across 23 countries, valued at approximately $1.3 billion. The portfolio illustrates the potential to connect international discussions with practical investment opportunities. Its value represents a project pipeline; delivery will depend on financing and implementation.

Mongolia’s Steppe Action Agenda reinforced that emphasis, bringing together priorities including rangeland management, nature-based infrastructure and the relationship between land and water.

The conference left further work ahead. Negotiations on several issues, including drought, will continue at COP18 in Egypt in 2028. The partnerships advanced in Ulaanbaatar must now translate into benefits for communities and landscapes.

For Mongolia, COP17 established a platform for that next phase. The government brought countries together, supported negotiations and placed the experience of the steppe within a global conversation about resilience.

The world came to Ulaanbaatar. Mongolia’s opportunity now is to carry that momentum from the conference halls to the land.

Tech leaders, including Yann LeCun, Nobel laureate Philippe Aghion and the CEOs of ElevenLabs and Lovable, call on the EU to secure a dedicated AI allocation in its 2028-2034 budget.

Dozens of European tech founders and scientists are warning that the window to compete in artificial intelligence is closing and the European Union’s next long-term budget will be crucial to deciding the continent’s place in the future.

The open letter, signed by 59 leaders, including Nobel laureate and economist Philippe Aghion, one of AI’s so-called godfathers Yann LeCun, and the heads of DeepL, OVHcloud, ElevenLabs and Lovable, argues Europe risks losing its technological sovereignty and competitiveness.

“We share a deep belief in Europe’s potential, but also a growing sense of alarm: the world is undergoing a technological revolution, and Europe is competing in it with a fraction of the capital, the compute, and the scaling capacity of its rivals. The gap is widening every quarter,” the letter reads.

China and the United States are battling to take the lead on the technology that promises to transform healthcare, manufacturing, and global economies. Countries that lead in AI will not only define global power but also grow their economies.

Titled ‘An Urgent Call: Europe Cannot Sleep Through the AI Revolution,’ the letter released on Wednesday says the talent and ambition already exist in Europe, but what is missing is the political will and capital to match them.

They warn negotiations on the EU budget for 2028-2034 are under way, and what is not secured during the talks will not exist before 2035.

The five AI demands

The letter sets out five demands. The first is simplification: the authors say Europe is right to protect safety and fundamental rights, but that this should not bury innovators in bureaucracy.

They welcome the first Digital Omnibus, a legislative package introduced to simplify, streamline, and reduce administrative burdens across the EU’s digital rulebook. However, they say it must not be the last step, and they want the ongoing review of the digital rulebook to produce binding simplification.

They also call on the EU to create a true 28th regime, so that a company can incorporate once and operate under one set of rules in every member state.

Scale and data

The second demand is to help European tech scale. Europe, the letter argues, is good at producing ideas but poor at capturing their benefits, because too many founders start companies in the United States or relocate there during later funding rounds.

They call for the channelling of Europe's large pool of private savings through pension funds and insurers into scale-up funds, completing the single market for capital, and having governments act as anchor customers for European technology.

The letter also calls for broad access to data, which they say matters as much as compute or capital.

Investment

The third ask is a reality check on investment. While there are investments in the EU’s AI "Gigafactories", they say AI needs more investment, as American companies alone are putting hundreds of billions of dollars into AI infrastructure this year.

To fund this, they call on European leaders to secure a dedicated and ambitious AI allocation within the European Competitiveness Fund and the next research framework programme.

Talent

The fourth ask is to retain Europe’s talent and calls for institutions for talent.

'Ambitious strategy'

The final demand is a change of mindset in Europe, saying that the continent can no longer be content with regulating technologies invented elsewhere; it must move from defence to offence and deliberately back European champions with the scale, capital and market access to compete globally.

“Europe can no longer be satisfied with simply regulating the technologies invented by others. We need a far more ambitious strategy for technological competition with the world.

"We must shift our mindset from playing defence to playing offence, and eventually to win,” the letter reads.

Euronews has reached out to the European Commission for comment.

Police in Bangladesh clashed with thousands of garment workers demanding higher basic wages on Wednesday amid weekslong chaos in the main export-earning industry in the country, police and media reports said.

Violence was also reported in the district of Gazipur, outside Dhaka, which is a major industrial zone.

Protesters also blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway and torched a police vehicle. Police fired tear gas and stun grenades during the violence.

The industry earns about $40 billion (€36 billion) a year from exports through the South Asian nation’s garment factories, which number around 2,500.

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 takas (€215), up from 12,500 takas (€89).

When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding positive relationship.

Trump said that during the unprecedented trilateral meeting on Thursday he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about ending Russia’s ongoing all-out war in Ukraine, declaring on Tuesday that “I think it’s very close to getting it done".

“We are going to have a good meeting on that," Trump said.

Beijing announced the trilateral meeting as “in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations” on the sidelines of the APEC meeting, while Putin said that he expected the summit to be “highly useful”.

Trump has signalled that he wants to take an improvised approach at the APEC summit, betting that his unscripted brand of diplomacy, based on personal relationships, can create a legacy by reshaping world affairs during his final two years in the White House.

Europe and the world will be watching as Trump meets with two of Washington's largest geopolitical rivals after relations with US’ historical allies such as Europe and Canada have turned sour over the last months.

Trump raised the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, which had not yet been confirmed by the time the US president arrived in China.

During his first in-person appearance at an APEC leaders meeting since 2017, Putin met his Chinese counterpart on Wednesday and took aim at what he called “instruments of economic dominance,” such as the sanctions imposed on Russia following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.

“Sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions” have “outlived their usefulness and have largely lost their intimidating effect,” Putin told a CEO summit on the sidelines of the APEC summit.

He highlighted his country’s desire to cultivate closer economic ties with the Asia-Pacific, saying the region accounts for more than half of its total trade.

Xi calls for open trade and equitable growth

In a speech on the sidelines of the APEC summit on Wednesday, the Chinese president told business executives that the Asia-Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth to remain stable and dynamic.

"China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access, but also go a step further. We will carry out reform in challenging areas such as rules, regulation, and standards,” Xi said, reiterating Beijing’s pledges to improve conditions for global investors.

"While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development,” he said.

“It has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation.”

Xi and other APEC leaders called for a more open approach, without directly criticising the US shift toward protecting its own markets.

Trump’s “America First” approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone, as Washington limits on Chinese access to cutting-edge US technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help to power artificial intelligence, are a constant source of strain with Beijing.

Trump is expected to seek to reinforce the US status as the world’s leading technology power.

His tariffs, intended to curb China's trade surplus, have done little to stop the progress of the world’s dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than it imported.

When answering reporters about US policies towards Beijing's access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that “we have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”

Trump’s emphasis on friendly relations with Xi may extend the trade truce reached last year after a series of tariff escalations.

Trump has also said that during his talks with Xi, he does not plan to bring up Taiwan, the leading manufacturer of advanced computer chips, including those designed by US companies, but expects Xi to push him on Taiwan’s sovereignty.

“I’m sure he’ll raise it,” Trump said. “I won’t have to raise it.”

The 21 APEC economies account for 60% of global economic activity, half of global trade and 40% of humanity. The leaders will meet behind closed doors on Thursday, while holding other meetings on the event’s sidelines.

APEC does not take binding decisions, but over 37 years it has served as a forum for building a consensus on cooperation and more open trade.

The APEC summit is showcasing Shenzhen, which China has transformed in the past four decades from a fishing village into a skyscraper-studded centre for export manufacturing and technology.

Higher fuel prices pushed UK inflation up from 3.5% in September to 3.6% in October. Diesel hit a record high, while prices for food and non-alcoholic drinks rose at their slowest pace in five years.

Annual inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October, up from 3.5% the previous month, largely driven by the jump in the cost of motor fuels.

"Inflation rose slightly in October, with fuel prices once again a major contributor to the increase in the annual rate," said Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Motor fuel prices rose by 33.2% in the year to October, up from 29.8% in September. It was the fastest rise since July 2022. Petrol prices rose to their highest level since August 2022, while diesel prices hit a record high.

Higher fuel prices meant transport contributed the most to the rise in the overall inflation rate. Transport prices rose by 7.5% in the year to October, up from 6.6% in September.

Meanwhile, inflation for food and non-alcoholic drinks eased to 0.9% from 1.3%, its lowest since September 2021.

Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was unchanged at 2.8%.

The overall consumer price index rose by 0.5% in October compared with the previous month.

Sanjay Raja, Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, said: "Overall, today’s print was far softer than we ourselves expected." He said food prices were rising slowly, although they were widely expected to rise faster in 2027.

What does this mean for interest rates?

"Today’s inflation data will give the Bank of England some breathing space," Raja said. He added that inflation was still uncomfortably high, but both the overall and core rates were 0.1 percentage points below the Bank’s forecasts. Services inflation, which held at 3.7%, was also lower than the Bank had expected.

The Bank raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% in early November to curb inflation. It was the first increase in more than three years.

"Looking beyond October, we still think the worst is yet to come," Raja said. He expects Ofgem’s cap on household energy prices to rise by more than 20% in January and food inflation to climb again. He also pointed to the expiry of two temporary tax cuts in July 2027, one on petrol and diesel and the other on household electricity in Great Britain.

The Bank of England’s November forecast put inflation at around 5% in mid-2027. In a separate scenario in which energy prices rose sharply and stayed high, the Bank projected that inflation could reach about 6.2% in the third quarter.

Raja expects inflation to peak well below the Bank’s forecast. He thinks higher energy costs will have less of an effect on wages and other prices than the Bank expects.

Raja said, "We see CPI pushing above 4% early next year – and sticking above 3% y/y all year."

He expects inflation to slow towards 3% by the end of 2027 as earlier energy price rises drop out of the annual comparison and gas prices ease. He said a sustained return to the Central Bank’s 2% target "looks unlikely before late 2028".

A decade after the Brexit referendum, Brussels and London are poised to deepen ties on trade, defence and energy, but draft summit conclusions seen by Euronews reveal lingering political divisions.

EU and UK leaders meet in Brussels on Friday for a pivotal summit that could mark the most decisive political break with the Brexit era, a decade after the referendum that drove the two sides apart.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has made rebuilding relations with Europe a political priority since taking office in July, has been openly critical of Brexit, describing the current relationship with the EU as "not good enough" and even floating the prospect of rejoining the bloc.

With Europe under growing pressure to take greater responsibility for its own security and boost its economic competitiveness, there is also a political imperative on both sides of the Channel to put years of acrimony behind them.

Brussels and London are expected to unveil a package of agreements covering trade, defence industry cooperation, agrifood standards, youth mobility, economic security and access to the EU electricity market.

Draft summit conclusions circulated to European governments on Tuesday evening shed light on how the EU and UK intend to forge closer ties than at any point since Britain left the bloc in 2020.

But the document, seen by Euronews, also reveals the limits of the rapprochement, with negotiators still haggling over several politically sensitive issues just days before the summit.

Bilateral agreements

The two sides have all but finalised an agreement to align agrifood standards, which would scrap existing border controls and certification requirements for “the vast majority” of animal and plant products traded between the UK and the EU from 1 March 2028.

They are also expected to confirm a deal linking the UK and EU Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), which would remove the need for carbon border levies on trade between them, although the draft statement sets no date for its application.

Sticking points remain over a deal integrating the UK into the EU electricity market. Britain has some of the highest energy prices in Europe, while Brussels wants to make access conditional on a financial contribution to the bloc’s funding for its poorest regions. Both sides commit to concluding negotiations in 2027.

The EU and UK are also set to launch a digital partnership in early 2027 covering secure connectivity, artificial intelligence and digital identities. However, a commitment to apply the EU's AI Act and Cyber Resilience Act to Northern Ireland under the Windsor Framework has been struck out.

Youth mobility

Youth mobility remains a key point of contention. EU countries want their students to receive equal treatment at British universities, notably on tuition fees, while the UK argues that it attracts far more European students than it sends to the continent.

The thorny question of fees has been moved into a parallel agreement. The draft statement currently contains two options: equal treatment for EU nationals or “significantly reduced undergraduate fees.”

The statement sets a clear timeline for the Youth Experience Scheme (TES), which would let young people live in each other’s territory for up to three years to work or study.

The aim is to seal the agreement by 2028 at the latest and have the scheme running by January 2030. The total number of participants has not been decided yet, although sources say it is likely to be around 100,000.

Defence integration

Defence industry cooperation has been a source of friction, with France pushing to restrict British firms' access to the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme over concerns about competition from across the Channel.

But the two sides are being pushed closer, as the US eyes a drawdown of its military presence in Europe, while also backing Ukraine’s war effort and attempting to fill the strategic gaps the Americans leave behind.

The UK has already been included in the Ukraine Support Loan, and the summit looks set to pave the way for closer defence industrial integration.

“Given the global security context, we intend to enhance exchanges on defence industrial issues and will identify ways to deepen capability collaboration, taking into account the objective of developing resilient European supply chains and capabilities and addressing critical capability gaps, including through the Capability Coalitions,” the text reads.

The Capability Coalitions allow EU member states to work together to address military shortfalls in strategic areas such as air defence, drones and ammunition.

Steel safeguards

Earlier this year, the EU adopted steel safeguards to counter Chinese overcapacity, which affected all exporters to the European market, including the UK.

The two sides now commit to exploring bilateral safeguards based on their respective quota allocations, to protect their industries from global overcapacity.

“A long-term sustainable solution for movement of UK originating steel to Northern Ireland would also be put in place,” the document states.

Economic security

London and Brussels will set up a dialogue on economic security, covering export controls, technology leakage in critical sectors and supply chain disruption.

A reference to coordination on market access, public procurement and subsidies has been removed. Discussions within the EU on whether a European preference in public procurement should also apply to the UK are still ongoing.

Notably, the EU wants the UK to ensure its national policies produce outcomes equivalent to the bloc’s, while London has proposed much softer language on protecting supply chains consistently and pre-empting circumvention.

Home affairs and migration

The EU's demand that the UK suspend its regime for deporting foreign national offenders has been dropped from the statement. Instead, the two sides commit to providing advance notice of such removals and exploring bilateral cooperation on prisoner transfers.

The two sides also acknowledge the difficulties law enforcement authorities face in obtaining electronic data from other jurisdictions. They commit to exploring ways “to reinforce mutual and reciprocal exchanges of data on criminal records of third country nationals, in the light of technical developments.”

The statement calls for more systematic, structured and reciprocal information exchange between EU member states and the UK to prevent migrant smuggling and human trafficking across the Channel, including by enabling the work of the EU border agency Frontex.

Claudia Sheinbaum met Chinese president Xi Jinping at the APEC summit.

Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum has asked Chinese President Xi Jinping for a panda during a meeting in China.

The Chapultepec zoo, in Mexico City, is home to Xin Xin, a 36-year-old female regarded as the only giant panda in the world that does not belong to China. She is the last descendant of a line of giant pandas that arrived in Mexico in 1975.

"Next year marks the 55th anniversary of relations between Mexico and China, a very important date," Sheinbaum, a known environmentalist, told reporters in Shenzhen.

"We spoke about advancing in the field of tourism and we also asked for a panda for the Chapultepec zoo as part of this cooperation," she explained on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. "So it was a very good, very cordial and very frank meeting," added the Mexican politician.

What is panda diplomacy?

In the 1940s China began sending pandas to different countries abroad to strengthen diplomatic ties. But since the 1980s, the pandas came with strings attached: they are loaned to other countries for fixed periods in return for a financial contribution that goes towards programmes to conserve the species in the wild.

The contributions seem to be working - in 2021, China removed pandas from its endangered species list.

Native to the temperate forests of East Asia, these large black-and-white mammals do not usually roam over long distances in the wild. However, many have been moved to zoos around the world as part of the 'panda diplomacy' programme, a strategy Beijing has used for decades to strengthen relations with other countries.

Mexico's story is an example of this diplomatic dimension. In 1975, China gave the country a pair of giant pandas, Ying Ying and Pe Pe. The Mexico City government has said that this gift was part of a diplomatic agreement that symbolised friendship and cooperation between the two countries.

Earlier this year, Beijing demanded the return of the two pandas it had in Japan, amid a diplomatic dispute that began after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested that Tokyo could intervene militarily if there were an attack on Taiwan.

Sheinbaum also told Xi on Tuesday that relations between Mexico and China are entering a "new era". For his part, the Chinese president called for raising bilateral ties to "a higher level" in view of the complex international situation.

It set off at a time when mobile phones were still science fiction. Nearly half a century later, Voyager 1 continues its journey through space.

It is an adventure that perfectly embodies one of NASA's slogans, "Making the impossible possible" ("Rendre possible l'impossible"), and a historic milestone confirmed by the space agency: at this precise moment, 11:16 CET, Voyager 1 is about 25.9 billion kilometres from Earth. No human-made object has ever travelled so far. What is even more remarkable is that this grand old lady of space exploration is still operating, nearly 50 years after leaving our planet.

A journey that began in 1977

It all started on 5 September 1977 at the Cape Canaveral Space Center in Florida. Mounted on top of a powerful Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket, Voyager 1 broke away from Earth with an ambitious mission: to explore the giant planets of the solar system. Its twin, Voyager 2, had actually set off earlier, on 20 August. But Voyager 1 followed a faster trajectory and eventually overtook it.

Today it is travelling at almost 61 000 km/h, about 17 kilometres per second. It gained this speed in particular thanks to the gravitational pull of the planets it flew past. In March 1979 it passed close to Jupiter, revealing its rings and the extraordinary volcanic activity on its moon Io. In November 1980 it flew over Saturn and carried out a close study of its spectacular rings and its moon Titan.

But instead of continuing to explore the other planets, Voyager 1 (source in French) then headed into the depths of space. In August 2012 it became the first human spacecraft to cross the heliopause, the boundary beyond which the solar wind no longer dominates the space environment. It thus entered interstellar space. Its twin Voyager 2 (source in French) joined it in 2018.

This short report from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (source in French) is well worth a look for space enthusiasts. It dates from the time and explains the missions of the two Voyager probes. The same goes for this NASA gallery (source in French), where you can see how it was built.

A golden record for extraterrestrials

On board, Voyager 1 is carrying something far more poetic than its scientific instruments: a golden record 30 centimetres in diameter, attached to its structure. Conceived in particular by the famous astronomer Carl Sagan, this record is a kind of business card for humanity, intended for any possible extraterrestrial civilisations.

It contains 115 images (source in French), greetings in 55 languages, sounds of nature, heartbeats, whale songs, laughter and a musical selection ranging from Bach to Chuck Berry. It even includes a message from the then US president, Jimmy Carter. A concentrated sample of terrestrial civilisation dispatched into the cosmic immensity.

A journey full of obstacles

After almost half a century in space, Voyager 1 is starting to show its age. In November 2023 a computer problem prevented it from transmitting its scientific data correctly. It took engineers several months to find a solution, working remotely on a computer designed in the 1970s.

In 2024 it was the thrusters that began to show signs of weakness, as tiny pipes gradually became clogged. The team then had to switch to another system to keep its antenna pointed towards Earth.

More recently, a drop in its power output, generated by the decay of plutonium, has forced NASA to switch off certain instruments to save energy.

In April 2026 a new scientific instrument was turned off. The probe nevertheless continues to send back data thanks to the equipment that is still working.

What will happen to it in the coming decades, and then the coming centuries?

Voyager 1 has no more planets to visit and now continues its journey through interstellar space. (source in French) Its trajectory will take it towards the Oort Cloud, the vast reservoir of comets surrounding our solar system. But it will take about 300 years to reach the inner part of the cloud, and perhaps 30 000 years to leave it completely, if it does not by chance collide with one of the comets.

In around 40 000 years the probe will pass at about 1.7 light-years from the star Gliese 445, a red dwarf in the constellation Camelopardalis. A very relative encounter on a cosmic scale, as it is not expected to come close enough to be captured by that system.

Long before that, Voyager 1 will probably have stopped communicating with Earth. Its energy reserves will eventually be too low to power its instruments and its radio transmitter.

But the probe will continue its journey. It could drift through the galaxy for millions or even billions of years. Its golden record may remain intact long after every trace of our civilisation and our solar system has disappeared.

There is a little of 2001: A Space Odyssey in this story, a hint of Star Trek and a great deal of human genius. Voyager 1 will probably never have an audience to applaud its achievement, nor any little green man to retrieve its golden record. Yet it continues on its way, silent, where none of our kind has ever gone. And that alone commands admiration.

Worldwide, more and more families are choosing to adopt a cat, and the global market for food, gadgets and merchandising is worth over one hundred billion euros, driving the pet economy.

A market worth more than one hundred billion euro, millions of new owners and rising consumption. No longer just pets, cats have become the driving force behind a global economic phenomenon known as Catnomics , which stretches from the United States to Japan and also includes Italy.

To give an idea of the scale of the phenomenon, it is enough to note that these felines alone account for 38.5% of all spending in the pet economy, according to a report by PW Consulting and data from the monitoring carried out by the Schesir Respect My Nature Index.

From Japan to Italy, more and more families are choosing to adopt a cat

In Japan alone, where the trend is known as "Nekonomics", the market in 2026 almost reached a value of 17 billion euro (3,000 billion yen) in cat cafés, gadgets and other products, according to Professor Katsuhiro Miyamoto of Kansai University.

In a survey, the Japan Pet Food Association reports that in 2025 Japanese people owned 8.8 million cats compared with 6.8 million dogs. According to the same report, over the lifetime of a cat a family spends on average almost 10,300 euro (1.8 million yen).

"The growth of Catnomics reflects a profound change in the way people experience their relationship with their cats: on the one hand they are increasingly seen as full members of the family, while on the other hand knowledge of their specific physiological needs, especially from a nutritional point of view, is often lacking," explains Giorgio Montefusco, Marketing & Trade Marketing Director at Schesir, "particularly in Italy, demand is rising for products able to combine quality, palatability and respect for the cat's physiological and behavioural needs".

Cats are also driving the pet economy in Europe

Europeans in general tend to prefer cats. According to the 2026 "Facts & Figures" report by FEDIAF EuropeanPetFood, in Europe in 2024 around 149 million households, 49%, had pets, for a total of 306 million pets, including 111 million cats and 91 million dogs.

Cat food generates the highest market value at 50%, followed by dog food at 46%, even though 58% of the pet food produced in Europe is for dogs and only 41% for cats.

Statista also appears to confirm this trend, noting that "in Europe overall, the number of cats has increased significantly since 2010. In 2024, the European Union alone was home to a large cat population, making them the most popular companion animals. The population of pet cats in the European Union also reflects the size of the pet products sector in this region".

France and Germany top the ranking of European countries with the most pet cats, followed by Italy, where the presence of felines is growing, with a 4.7% increase in adoptions from 2022 to 2025, bringing the total number of cats in households to eleven million, compared with 10.2 million three years earlier.

Annual spending on cat food in Italy is around 2.35 billion euro, according to the ASSALCO-Zoomark 2026 report, which stresses that this segment accounts for 56% of the pet food market for dogs and cats, with annual growth of 4.3%, reports Agi.

In the US it is Gen Z men who are driving the rise in cat adoptions

The sector is also booming in the United States, where the rise in the number of adopted cats is driven by Gen Z men, according to a report by the American Pet Products Association. Men account for 43% of cat owners in the US, and among Gen Z the number of adopted cats has increased by 27% in just one year.

The number of US households that have chosen to have a cat has reached 53 million, about 39% of the total, a 5% increase between 2024 and 2025. The report also notes that since 2018 the share of households with at least three cats has risen, with an increase of 45%.

This trend has taken hold in China as well, where the cat market is growing much faster than the dog market and individual spending on cats has risen. In urban centres there are 72.9 million cats compared with 53.4 million dogs, with the economic value of the cat market increasing by 5.2% compared with 3.2% for dogs.

But the market linked to cats is not only expanding, it is also undergoing several transformations. Beyond spending on food and veterinary visits, more and more money goes towards the ageing of cats, an area known as the "Silver cat economy" that is growing rapidly in Hong Kong.

There are more and more cat owners choosing to invest in the longevity of their pet, a development that confirms that the bond with cats is taking on an increasingly important role in the international pet market.
